text:
The Roadless Rule was enacted to protect wild lands from road construction, logging, and any other development. The 58 million acres of wild land needs to remain wild. Once it is logged and developed, there is no getting it back. These forests need to be protected for the American people and future generations, to preserve parts of the earth in its natural state. These lands need to be protected from timber and mineral extraction to preserve habitats for thousands of species, some of them endangered. Climate change continues to elevate average world temperatures, creating more severe storms and wildfires. Old-growth forests are one of human’s greatest allies against climate change by being a massive carbon sink for the greenhouse gas, carbon dioxide. So, instead of protecting old-growth forests, investing in renewable energies, and moving towards regenerative agriculture, all of which have the potential to slow, or even reverse the effects of climate change, the Trump administration and the secretary of agriculture Brooke Rollins are attempting to rescind the Roadless Rule. And it is all being done on a false narrative that building roads through these protected areas will help combat wildfires. 

The truth is, wildfires are four times more likely to occur within 50 meters of a road than the forests protected by the Roadless Rule. The reason for this, is that wildfires are typically ignited by humans. And where you have roads, you have humans. Furthermore, old-growth forests develop a resilience to wildfires by having more moisture retention, more species diversity, and ecological complexity. Clearcutting the old-growth forests for roads creates secondary forest growth, which has much less resilience to wildfires. These forests are not able to retain as much moisture and there is less species diversity. This results in much more intense wildfires that cannot be contained. So not only will roads through these protected forests not help prevent wildfires, but they will make things much worse.

Justification for rescinding the Roadless Rule points towards executive orders from President Trump; specifically, EO 14192 Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation, EO 14225 Immediate Expansion of American Timber Production, and EO 14154 Unleashing American Energy. To sum this up, Trump has created an absolute mess, and now protected national forests will have to make up for it. To put it another way, all of the jobs created and investments made for clean energy in the Inflation Reduction Act have essentially been taken away. And then to make matters worse, tariffs for Canadian lumber have been increased to 35%. Canada has the forests to supply the lumber needed for American demand, but the US does not. Neither of these moves make any sense logistically, economically, or sustainably. What is really happening is the wealthy become even more wealthy by a system rigged by the White House, and at the expense of our natural resources and the future generations of America.

So many Americans rely on protected lands for hunting, finishing, and recreating. My wife and I just completed a 200-mile backpacking trip, hiking most of the John Muir Trail. If you haven’t experienced something similar, it is an absolutely incredible adventure. The trail took us through some of the most beautiful mountain landscapes in America. It was also very secluded and remote. We didn’t see a road or a vehicle until day 14 of our 16-day trek, and it is because of protections like the Roadless Rule that made this possible. Being fully immersed in nature like this only strengthens my desire to protect these special and undeveloped places. My hope is that these places will continue to be there for future generations. 

President Theodore Roosevelt said, “the time has come to inquire seriously what will happen when our forests are gone, when the coal, the iron, the oil, and the gas are exhausted, when the soils have still further impoverished and washed into the streams, polluting the rivers, denuding the fields and obstructing navigation.” What will we do then? That is exactly where we are heading.

" In 2001, the Roadless Area Conservation Rule established a single, nationwide set of prohibitions intended to provide lasting protection for inventoried roadless areas within the National Forest System in the context of multiple-use management." I believe, as an individual who regularly utilizes these protected lands, that they deserve to be preserved as a resource to mother nature. 

 The quoted statement here "allow for active management to respond to changing and localized conditions, such as increasing wildfire risk, the spread of insect and disease infestations, and the need for community protection in the wildland-urban interface." does not address the root of the issue with removing these protections; that being the destruction of America's native wildlife, and further encroachment on native species via logging and industrialization which will undoubtedly follow the recinding of protections. 

In the statement quoted here "In Executive Order 14225, Immediate Expansion of American Timber Production, the President declared that “the United States has an abundance of timber resources that are more than adequate to meet our domestic timber production needs, but heavy-handed Federal policies have prevented full utilization of these resources.” I believe as an individual that sustainability simply cannot be achieved when the plan is to progress this order. 

The natural beauty of our country has continuously been threatened by the president and members of government. When my children and their children's children are growing up, I want them to experience and understand New England's national forests and parks. To allow encroachment upon these protected lands is to allow the greedy and unpatriotic among us to plunder as they please, and leave nothing in their wake.

I am a United States citizen and a co-owner of the lands this rule governs. I oppose the rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule in its entirety. I do not support rescinding any portion of it, and I do not support replacing it with forest-level discretion that removes the national protection these acres currently hold.

The proposal is presented as a wildfire measure. The record does not support that framing.

Road access is not what limits fuels reduction. The agency has treated only a small fraction of inventoried roadless acreage since 2014, but it has also failed to treat vast portions of the 149 million acres of National Forest System land that are already roaded and accessible. If access were the binding constraint, the treated acreage in accessible areas would be far higher than it is. The actual constraints are appropriations, workforce capacity, burn windows, NEPA staffing, and a deferred maintenance backlog on existing roads that the agency already cannot fund. Rescinding this rule addresses none of those.

There are established methods for reducing hazardous fuels without permanent road construction. Prescribed fire, managed natural ignitions, hand crews, aerial and pack-supported delivery, and temporary access under existing exceptions are all available today. The 2001 rule already permits road construction where needed for public health and safety. Land managers are not locked out. They are underfunded.

New roads also introduce fire risk rather than removing it. The large majority of wildfire ignitions in this country are human-caused, and human ignition density tracks with road access. Building permanent road networks into currently unroaded terrain increases the number of ignition sources in the exact landscapes the proposal claims to be protecting. It also fragments habitat, degrades the headwaters that supply drinking water to millions of people, and spreads invasive species along road corridors.

The proposal's own stated alignment tells the real story. The rescission is justified by reference to Executive Order 14225 on timber production, Executive Order 14154 on energy, and Executive Order 14153 on Alaska resource extraction. Those are commodity access directives. A rule genuinely motivated by community fire protection would be aligned with wildland urban interface priorities, not with timber output targets and energy leasing. The fire language is the packaging. Extraction is the product.

The public has already answered this question. The 2001 rule was finalized after roughly 1.6 million public comments, the largest response to a federal rulemaking at that time, and the overwhelming majority supported protection. Every subsequent attempt to unwind it has drawn the same response. This is not a partisan preference. Hunters, anglers, backcountry hunters and anglers organizations, ranchers, hikers, rural water districts, tribal governments, and outfitters have all defended these protections, and they do not vote as a bloc. Support for keeping wild country wild crosses every political line in this country. What does not cross those lines is the small set of interests that stand to profit from the timber, mineral, and energy access this rescission would open.

That is my frustration, stated plainly. Do not tell the public that this is about beetles and brush when the rule is anchored to timber and energy directives and when the tools to manage beetles and brush already exist without roads. The last unroaded quarter of our national forest system is not a management inconvenience. It belongs to all of us, and once it is roaded, it does not come back.

I ask that the Forest Service withdraw this proposed rule and retain the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule in full.

I am writing in opposition to rescinding the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. According to the USDA Forest Service (2026a), the proposed rollback of the Roadless Rule would increase flexibility in management, including where and when to reduce wildfire risk based on local conditions. However, between 1992 and 2024, wildfires were four times more likely to start near roads than in roadless tracts and over 90% of fires nationwide ignite within half a mile of a road (Aplet et al. 2026). The California Southern Zone Forests & Human Caused Fire Ignition Analysis found that two thirds of fires were caused by humans. According to research from the USDA Forest Service, 95% of wildfires are started by humans (Avitt 2026), indicating that increasing access would likely increase wildfire risk. In addition, Roadless Rule exceptions already exist. Managers can thin forests, conduct prescribed burns, and build temporary roads for emergencies. A GIS analysis by the Wilderness Society (2025) found that less than 5% of roadless acres are near the Wildland-Urban Interface, meaning these are areas where homes and communities are not vulnerable to wildfire damage. 

Repealing the Roadless Rule would threaten protections for nearly 58.5 million acres of undeveloped backcountry forestlands—about one-third of all U.S. national forests. These protections have kept forests intact by preventing new road construction for large-scale logging, mining, or oil-and-gas drilling. When implemented, more than 95% of the 1.6 million comments collected spoke in favor of this rule that helps ensure habitat connectivity, clean water, and outstanding recreational opportunities in our national forests (Federal Register 2001). 

I have worked as a fisheries and wildlife biologist for nearly 20 years. For the vast majority of wildlife listed as threatened or endangered, habitat loss and fragmentation is listed as the primary cause. According to assessments by the U.S. Forest Service compiled during the creation of the Roadless Rule, roadless areas function as biological strongholds for many species, including numerous species protected by the Endangered Species Act (Federal Register 2001). 

Further, national forests are the headwaters for America’s rivers, providing clean drinking water to more than 60 million people in 3,400 communities across 33 states (US Forest Service 2026b). Roads are a major source of water pollution; by keeping these headwaters intact, the Roadless Rule protects safe, clean drinking water for cities. Numerous studies show that intact forests create buffers around waterways, slowing rain and runoff, filtering pollutants from water, and refilling underground aquifers (e.g., Mckie 2006).

Older, mature forests in roadless areas are also carbon sinks, storing vast amounts of carbon dioxide and buffering climate change impacts. Logging removes these natural defenses, worsening climate change and wildfire risk, while reducing biodiversity and water resilience (DellaSala et al. 2022). 

These are also valuable recreation areas, which support local economies. Areas protected by the Roadless Rule provide hunting, fishing, climbing, biking, hiking, whitewater rafting, and camping opportunities.  

The U.S. Forest Service already manages a 370,000-mile road system with a multi-billion-dollar backlog in maintenance. Adding new roads in backcountry forests will only deepen the taxpayer burden while further degrading ecosystems. 

The Roadless Rule is one of America’s most popular conservation measures, and remains widely supported today. Therefore, I urge you to protect 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule.

text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

The smoke rolling off the nearest mountain for most of August is not an abstraction. It settled over everything, made the air awful, and made plain what is already happening to the forests I hike in to get away from city life and find stretches of nature that haven't been ruined by corporate greed. Rescinding the Roadless Area Conservation Rule would accelerate exactly that ruin, and the agency's own record does not support the move.

On wildfire, the agency's own text states: "Building a road into a forest at high risk from uncharacteristic wildfire effects could increase the incidence of human-caused fires. A human-caused wildland fire is nearly five times more likely to occur on essentially roaded lands than on essentially unroaded lands." The proposal nonetheless justifies rescission partly on fuels management grounds. I ask that the agency explain how this proposal departs from that prior finding and reconcile it with the ignition data in its own draft environmental impact statement, which reports far higher fire density on roaded land than inside the affected roadless areas.

Water is the next problem. My area's water supply depends on clean runoff from mountains and streams, and the agency's own analysis acknowledges that roads and their facilities can produce up to 90 percent of the sediment from a timber sale. Fewer than 12 percent of the watersheds fed by roadless areas have impaired streams today. Opening those areas to roads and logging is not only ecologically dangerous, it is, to use the plainest word, stupid, given what is already at stake for downstream communities. The agency must explain what analysis supports the conclusion that expanded road access is compatible with protecting water quality in those watersheds.

The economics do not close the case for rescission either. The agency's own record states that "the total timber volume affected by this rule is less than 0.5 percent of total United States production, and the total oil and gas production from all National Forest System lands is currently about 0.4 percent of the current national production." The agency's own cost-benefit analysis projects timber revenue to the Forest Service of $5.2 to $11.4 million a year against recreation losses of at least $6.1 million a year, with a net present value spanning -$92 million to +$199 million. The Forest Service already carries a $6.9 billion maintenance backlog on its existing road system. The agency must reconcile the proposal with those figures and explain on the record how an action whose own analysis cannot establish a net benefit justifies expanding that road system further.

The argument that state-by-state approaches can substitute for a national rule has been tested before and found wanting. The agency has itself acknowledged dissatisfaction with a nationwide approach, and the Ninth Circuit has already reviewed what happened when the national rule was replaced with state-specific petitions. That prior effort failed in court. The agency should address its own prior finding that local decision-making can incrementally erode nationally significant roadless values, and explain how this proposal avoids the deficiencies identified in that litigation.

Finally, the statutory authority question has already been answered by a federal appellate court. The record contains a holding that reads: "Exercising jurisdiction pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1291, we REVERSE the district court’s order granting Plaintiffs declaratory relief and issuing a permanent injunction, and REMAND the case for the district court to vacate the permanent injunction." The Tenth Circuit concluded that the 2001 rule was within the authority Congress granted under the Organic Act and the Multiple-Use Sustained-Yield Act and did not create de facto wilderness. The agency's position that the rule exceeded its statutory authority needs to be squared with that holding, and the basis for any contrary view stated plainly.

I oppose this rescission and urge the agency to keep the 2001 rule in place.

Sincerely,
Edward Flynn
Vancouver, WA 98662

Re: Special Areas; Roadless Area Conservation — RIN 0596-AD66, Docket FS-2025-0001
I am writing as a North Carolina resident to oppose the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule and to support retaining the rule in its current form (the No Action alternative).
Roadless areas are valuable precisely because they are undeveloped. Once a road is built or a stand is harvested, the roadless character of that landscape is gone, and no subsequent planning decision restores it. That asymmetry — permanent loss on one side, modest and uncertain gain on the other — argues for keeping the national protection in place.
The proposal’s own analysis supports this. It estimates that the increase in national sawtimber harvest would be in the range of 5 to 10 percent, that management opportunities would be “modest and localized,” and that recreationists could lose roughly $6.1 million in annual economic benefit, with tradeoffs for quiet, remote, and self-reliant recreation. It also acknowledges a $6.9 billion deferred maintenance backlog for existing Forest Service roads and bridges. Adding road mileage to a system the agency cannot currently maintain is not a sound use of limited funds.
In North Carolina, the inventoried roadless areas of the Nantahala and Pisgah National Forests supply clean headwaters, connected habitat for wildlife, and the backcountry that draws visitors to the western part of our state. These lands are part of what makes North Carolina distinctive, and the recreation and tourism economy they support is durable in a way that a one-time timber entry is not.
I ask the Department to withdraw the proposed rescission and retain 36 CFR part 294, subpart B.

text: It is not reasonable to assume, as the Department does here, that recession of the rule will have only a "modest" impact on the environment due to the likelihood that new roads will only result in around .5 mile distance from existing roads. The Department has failed to consider the incremental impact that adding new access has on wildlife segmentation. In addition, one half-mile of road surface added over the entire breath of the landscape that the roadless rule covers, has not been considered. Similarly, the combined impact of new roads in conjunction with the impact to the environment created by the Department's new "access management regulations"(see 36 CFR Parts 212 and 261) which presume motorized access is allowed unless otherwise prohibited has not been considered. Again, the incremental impact of presuming motorized access, combined with the addition of new roads for additional access to existing roads creates impacts that the Department has not considered. That is, even new roads less that .5 mile from existing roads will have more than a modest impact on wildlife habitat segmentation and disruption in conjunction with the Department's concurrent new rule to presume access to new roads. I am a hunter, hiker and climber in Washington State and I oppose recession of the roadless rule.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, RIN 0596-AD66, and urge the USDA to select the No Action Alternative and retain the existing rule.

The Roadless Rule provides consistent, nationwide protection for approximately 58.5 million acres of National Forest System land. Removing that protection would create opportunities for additional road construction, timber harvesting, and industrial development in some of our country’s remaining undeveloped forests. Once these areas are fragmented or damaged, restoring them to their original condition may be difficult or impossible.

These lands are not simply unused spaces awaiting development. They provide wildlife habitat, protect watersheds and water quality, store carbon, and give Americans access to quiet outdoor recreation. These benefits belong to the public, including future generations, and should not be sacrificed for short-term commercial interests.

The USDA’s own proposal acknowledges that rescission could cause noise, visible infrastructure, temporary closures, conflicts among recreational users, and losses in economic benefits associated with recreation. It also acknowledges that future changes to forest plans could increase the areas where roads and timber harvesting are allowed. That is precisely why the existing nationwide protection remains necessary. Depending on separate local planning decisions does not provide the same consistent or lasting safeguard.

Rescission could also shift the burden of repeatedly defending individual areas onto local communities, Tribal governments, conservation organizations, and ordinary citizens. The USDA’s summary states that the majority of Tribal governments consulted oppose rescission and have raised concerns involving Tribal sovereignty, sacred sites, traditional gathering areas, water quality, subsistence resources, and the ecological health of ancestral homelands. Those concerns deserve meaningful consideration before any national protection is removed.

As a mother, I believe we have a responsibility to leave our children more than damaged land and explanations about why short-term development was prioritized over permanent natural resources. Public forests belong to the American people, and their ecological and recreational value cannot be measured only by what can be extracted from them.

Local flexibility can still exist through the Roadless Rule’s current exceptions and other lawful forest-management tools. Complete rescission is unnecessarily broad and removes an important baseline of protection.

Please reject the proposed removal of 36 CFR Part 294, Subpart B, retain the 2001 Roadless Rule, and select the No Action Alternative. Protecting these lands is an investment in wildlife, clean water, outdoor recreation, Tribal communities, climate resilience, and future generations.

Public Comment: Opposition to Proposed Rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule as Applied to the Pisgah and Nantahala National Forests, North Carolina
Submitted to: U.S. Department of Agriculture / U.S. Forest Service
Docket: Proposed Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule (36 CFR Part 294)
Re: Draft Environmental Impact Statement, filed August 18, 2026
To the U.S. Department of Agriculture and U.S. Forest Service:
I am writing to formally oppose the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, and specifically its application to the nearly 152,000 acres of Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs) within the Pisgah and Nantahala National Forests in North Carolina.
Retaining the Roadless Rule as currently written is not merely the least-harmful option among several — it is the alternative that best serves the long-term health of these forests. Intact, unfragmented forest is more resilient to pests, disease, and severe weather; it protects the headwater streams that supply drinking water downstream; and it preserves the unbroken habitat corridors that many of the region's most sensitive species depend on. Every one of the stated objectives behind this proposal — forest health, wildfire resilience, and effective local management — is better achieved by preserving the rule than by rescinding it, for the reasons detailed below.

text:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule as it applies to the approximately 44.7 million acres of inventoried roadless areas on National Forest System lands. These lands matter to me because they hold old-growth trees that took centuries to grow and cannot be replaced once they're gone. That kind of loss is permanent in a way no replanting program can undo.
Background
This comment addresses the proposed rule published August 20, 2026, and the accompanying draft Environmental Impact Statement, which would rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule (66 FR 3244, 36 CFR Subpart B) and its prohibitions on road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas.
Analysis
For twenty-five years, the 2001 Roadless Rule has protected roadless areas from road building and commercial timber harvest, with the limited exceptions the rule already provides for wildfire risk reduction and other management needs. The proposed rescission would remove that baseline protection across nearly 45 million acres. I live in Colorado, where our own 2012 state-specific roadless rule already protects our forests, so I have no direct stake in this rule. I'm commenting because I care about the same protections holding for the 44.7 million acres in other states that don't have that safeguard.
The agency's stated rationale centers on wildfire management flexibility. That is a legitimate concern, but the existing rule already permits road construction and vegetation management for wildfire risk reduction in roadless areas. A full rescission goes well beyond what wildfire mitigation requires, and opens these areas to road construction and timber harvest for purposes unrelated to fire risk. 
Roadless areas provide drinking water source protection, intact wildlife habitat and migration corridors, and backcountry recreation access that roaded, managed timber lands do not replicate. The proposed rule and draft EIS should more fully account for these values, several of which are difficult to monetize but are not for that reason less real.
Recommendations
Withdraw the proposed full rescission and retain the 2001 Roadless Rule's core protections.

I strongly oppose the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (RIN 0596-AD66; Docket FS-2025-0001). I respectfully urge the Forest Service to retain the Rule and reject the proposed rescission.

The 2001 Roadless Rule provides an important national baseline protecting some of the last remaining large, undeveloped landscapes within the National Forest System. The Forest Service estimates that inventoried roadless areas encompass approximately 58.5 million acres, while the 2001 Rule provides protections across approximately 44.7 million acres. These lands provide benefits that cannot simply be recreated after roads and intensive development have fragmented them.

The proposal itself recognizes the environmental risks associated with rescission. The accompanying analysis acknowledges that increased road construction, road reconstruction, and timber harvesting could adversely affect scenic values, water quality, fisheries, wildlife, and recreational opportunities. These are not hypothetical or insignificant values. Roadless watersheds provide clean water, intact habitat, opportunities for primitive and non-motorized recreation, and landscape connectivity that become increasingly important as development and climate-related pressures increase.

I am particularly concerned with the proposal’s reliance on transferring decision-making from a national conservation standard to individual forest-level planning. Local decision-making is valuable, but roadless areas often provide benefits that extend far beyond the boundaries of a particular forest or local community. A national minimum standard prevents cumulative, incremental losses from occurring simply because individual decisions appear reasonable when considered in isolation.

The proposal also argues that rescission is necessary to address wildfire, forest health, insects, and disease. However, removing broad roadless protections should not be treated as synonymous with effective wildfire or forest-health management. The existence of a roadless area does not prevent all forms of active management, because the existing Rule contains exceptions. If particular management actions are necessary to protect communities, ecosystems, or public safety, those actions should be evaluated individually rather than eliminating nationwide protections for millions of acres.

Road construction is also not a reversible management decision in practical terms. Roads fragment habitat, facilitate additional human access and development, alter drainage and erosion patterns, and can permanently change the character of previously undeveloped landscapes. Once a road network is established, restoring an area to its previous condition can be extremely difficult or impossible.

The Forest Service should also give substantial weight to the recreational and cultural value of maintaining genuinely wild landscapes. Hiking, backpacking, hunting, fishing, wildlife viewing, climbing, and other forms of low-impact recreation depend on the continued existence of large areas where development remains limited. These opportunities have economic and social value to surrounding communities while also providing benefits that cannot be measured solely through timber or mineral production.

I am also concerned that the proposed rescission places too much emphasis on short-term economic opportunities while undervaluing long-term public benefits. National forests belong to the American public, and management decisions should preserve the full range of ecological, recreational, scenic, watershed, wildlife, and cultural values for future generations.

The Forest Service’s own environmental analysis recognizes that rescission could result in increased development and associated impacts to water quality, fisheries, wildlife, scenery, and recreation. Those acknowledged risks provide a compelling reason to retain the existing national protections rather than remove them.

If the Department believes changes to the Roadless Rule are necessary, I encourage it to pursue narrowly tailored amendments that address demonstrated management problems while maintaining strong protections against unnecessary road construction and commercial development in roadless areas.

For these reasons, I respectfully request that the Forest Service reject the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule and retain the nationwide protections contained in 36 CFR part 294, Subpart B.

Protecting these remaining roadless landscapes is not merely about preventing development today. It is about preserving options, ecological resilience, clean water, wildlife habitat, recreation, and irreplaceable wild places for generations of Americans who will never have the opportunity to restore what is permanently lost.

As a resident of New Mexico and a person who values and loves our national forests and public lands, I am writing to comment on the draft EIS that the USDA/USFS has published for comment. (Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, 36 CFR Part 294 RIN 0596-AD66.)

I retired from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) as a project manager and enforcement officer. In my duties, I read, wrote, reviewed, and commented on Environmental Assessments (EA) and Environmental Impact Statements (EIS) and other documents under NEPA. 

The proposed rescission would open 58.5 million acres of wild national forest nationwide to road building and logging, including nearly a quarter of New Mexico's Gila National Forest. Impact of the Roadless Rule Rescission in New Mexico: The rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule will significantly affect the management of national forests in New Mexico in a detrimental way.
    • Total Acres Affected Nationwide: 58.5 million acres
    • Specific Impact in New Mexico: The rule protects 1.6 million acres of the National Forest System in New Mexico. Nearly a quarter of New Mexico's Gila National Forest will be opened to road building and logging.
This rescission would allow for new development activities such as resource extraction in areas that were previously protected under the Roadless Rule, negatively impacting wildlife habitats, water sources, and recreational opportunities in the region. Repealing the rule will increase light pollution, harm wildlife, damage watersheds, and impede Indigenous cultural practices, all in service of profit for timber companies and other extractive interests.
Economic Impact: Logging in New Mexico's national forests can provide economic benefits by supporting local jobs and contributing to the economy through timber production. However, outdoor recreation in these forests generates significantly more economic value, contributing over $13 billion to the U.S. economy and supporting more than 205,000 jobs annually. 

The Department of Agriculture cited the need to increase forest and wildfire management and boost the pace of resource extraction as reasons for revoking the Roadless Rule. Research, however, contradicts the government’s claim that building more roads will help fight wildfires. A 2020 Forest Service study concluded, after nearly 20 years of monitoring data, that more roads do not lead to better forest health through increased fire-management activity. More roads could actually lead to more human-caused fires due to increased accessibility.

Our public lands belong to all of us. “Boosting resource extraction” is not a valid reason to rescind the Roadless Rule. As cited above, favoring resource extraction over recreational values makes no economic, environmental, or moral sense. The administration is intent on “reducing regulatory burdens,” but regulations help keep our public lands safe and accessible for all.

I join with our entire New Mexico congressional delegation and the tribal nations of New Mexico in urging USDA to keep the Roadless Rule. The No Action Alternative should be the USDA’s choice. Keep the Roadless Rule in place, for New Mexico, and for the country.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

I am an avid hiker, and some of my happiest and most meaningful experiences have come from spending time outdoors. I regularly hike in Virginia and Pennsylvania, and I recently had the chance to hike in Utah as well. Being in these landscapes reminds me how rare and valuable truly wild places are. There is something irreplaceable about walking through a quiet forest, seeing uninterrupted views, and knowing that the land around you has not been carved up by roads or development.

Rescinding the Roadless Rule would place millions of acres of national forest land at greater risk of road construction, logging, habitat fragmentation, erosion, invasive species, and the loss of the quiet and solitude that make these places special. However, I do not believe those concerns require eliminating the Roadless Rule nationwide. The existing Rule already allows exceptions for legitimate management needs. If additional flexibility is necessary, it should be addressed through careful, narrowly targeted changes rather than by removing a broad protection that has safeguarded these lands for decades.

These areas matter for far more than recreation. They protect wildlife habitat, clean water, biodiversity, scenic beauty, and ecological connections across large landscapes. They also give people the chance to experience nature in a way that is becoming increasingly difficult to find.

I want future generations to be able to hike through wild forests, stand on quiet overlooks, and experience the same sense of wonder that I have been fortunate enough to experience in Virginia, Pennsylvania, Utah, and beyond. We should not trade away that legacy for short-term development opportunities.

Please select the No Action alternative, retain the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, and reject the proposed removal of 36 CFR part 294, Subpart B.

As a botanist and conservationist, I am opposed to the rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule. The Forest Service lists “conserving the environment for generations to come” as one of its main objectives, and it invites Americans to help “strike a balance and make decisions in the best interest of the public lands and the public” (Meet the Forest Service | US Forest Service). I believe that protecting 58.5 million acres of inventoried roadless areas is in the best interest of the public lands and American people.
	The proposed rescission argues that local land managers “are best positioned to make decisions about inventoried roadless areas because they understand the unique ecological, economic, and social needs of their communities” (https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2026-16965/p-15). Under the 2001 Roadless Rule, specifically 36 CFR Part 294, Subpart B, a petition process is laid out for states to request special exemptions for land management purposes. States have had the opportunity to petition for these exemptions since 2006. If they needed to more closely manage roadless areas, they probably would have done so by now. As it stands, the Forest Service is unable to maintain all existing roads, and construction needs were backlogged by “over $8.6 billion in FY2023” (Maintaining Infrastructure | US Forest Service). Building more roads would add unnecessary economic strain to an already understaffed and overworked agency. Finally, in the original 2001 Roadless Rule record of decision, 63 FR 3244, it is noted that “local land management planning efforts may not always recognize the national significance of inventoried roadless areas and the values they represent in an increasingly developed landscape. If management decisions for these areas were made on a case-by-case basis at a forest or regional level, inventoried roadless areas and their ecological characteristics and social values could be incrementally reduced through road construction and certain forms of timber harvest” (https://www.federalregister.gov/d/01-726/p-71). The Forest Service is responsible for conserving our national public lands where individual land managers are incapable of seeing the bigger picture.
	The proposed rescission states that “the Secretary of Agriculture has broad authority under statutes such as the Organic Administration Act of 1897 and the Multiple-Use Sustained-Yield Act of 1960 to manage the National Forest System for a variety of uses” (https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2026-16965/p-17). Of the 193 million acres of land within the National Forest System, only 58.5 million are inventoried roadless areas, making up less than 30% of the total land. The other 70% of National Forest System land is used for recreation, timber harvest, grazing land, and other uses. Conservation is just as important a use of the land as anything else. 160 million Americans visit National Forest System land every year (By the Numbers | US Forest Service). Our wild lands make our country special, and American citizens know this to be true. We need to protect them so that future generations can visit National Forests as well.
Rescinding the rule would put our natural resources, including clean drinking water and intact ecosystems, in jeopardy. Growing up in North Carolina, I remember when a Duke Energy Plant released coal ash into the Dan River in 2014. For years since the leak, toxic chemicals including mercury, arsenic, and lead have been found in the water (cerc.usgs.gov/orda_docs/CaseDetails?ID=984). This spill made many North Carolinians sick and destroyed ecosystems along the river, including habitat for rare plants like Cardamine micranthera, a federally listed species. If the Roadless Rule is rescinded, oil, gas, and coal companies will have more opportunities to exploit public land and threaten sensitive plant and animal species. The resulting environmental degradation could have significant negative impacts on human and ecosystem health. The 2001 Roadless Rule protects untouched land from development, and in turn, it keeps us all healthy and allows us to enjoy the beauty of our public lands and biodiversity.
In summary, the Forest Service is responsible for protecting national public lands from degradation and for mixed uses, including conservation. The economic and environmental impacts are not worth rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule. I urge you to follow Alternative 1 (No Action) when deciding on the proposed rule.

I am commenting on the proposed rescission of 36 CFR Part 294, Subpart B 

Last summer I hiked a trail in Sequoia National Park where the only sound was water over granite and wind through ancient redwood trees. No roads. No trucks. No chainsaws. Just a forest that has been growing, undisturbed, for centuries. That kind of place is rare now, and it is beautiful in a way that no photograph or description can fully capture.
Please keep the Roadless Rule.

The Roadless Area Conservation Rule protects 58.5 million acres of exactly that kind of place. I'm asking you to keep it.

Beyond the beauty, the practical case is strong. Roads are the single greatest driver of habitat fragmentation in the West. I don't ask for a new rule. I ask that you leave the one that works in place. Let these forests keep being what they are — wild, quiet, and worth the trouble of getting to.

Thank you for considering this.

Public Comment on 36 CFR Part 294 – Roadless Rule (RIN 0596-AD66)
Docket ID: 2026-16965

To the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Forest Service,
To the Editor of the Federal Register,
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to strongly support the Roadless Rule as outlined in 36 CFR Part 294 (RIN 0596-AD66). This rule is a cornerstone of conservation in the United States, protecting over 58 million acres of wild, roadless national forests from logging, roadbuilding, and industrial development. These lands are irreplaceable for their ecological, cultural, and economic value—and their preservation is essential for current and future generations.

Why the Roadless Rule Must Be Upheld and Strengthened
1. Ecological and Climate Benefits
The Roadless Rule safeguards critical habitats for endangered and threatened species, including:

Grizzly bears (Ursus arctos horribilis)
Canada lynx (Lynx canadensis)
Pacific salmon (Oncorhynchus spp.)
Northern spotted owl (Strix occidentalis caurina)

These areas also serve as carbon sinks, storing vast amounts of carbon dioxide in old-growth forests and preventing the release of stored carbon that occurs with logging and road construction. In an era of climate crisis, preserving intact forests is not just beneficial—it is necessary.

2. Clean Water for Communities
Roadless areas are vital for clean water. They:

Filter and store water in headwaters, ensuring safe drinking water for millions downstream.
Prevent erosion and sedimentation, which can degrade rivers and streams.
Protect watersheds that support agriculture, fisheries, and local economies.
For example, the Tongass National Forest in Alaska, the largest intact temperate rainforest in the world, provides clean water for 116 communities, including Indigenous peoples who rely on these lands for subsistence and cultural practices.

3. Cultural and Spiritual Significance
For Indigenous communities, roadless areas hold deep cultural and spiritual significance. These lands are tied to:

Traditional hunting and gathering grounds.
Sacred sites and ancestral homelands.
Oral histories and cultural practices passed down for generations.
The Roadless Rule honors Tribal sovereignty and ensures that these lands remain intact for future generations to connect with their heritage.

4. Economic Value for Future Generations
Roadless areas support local economies through:

Tourism and recreation (hiking, fishing, hunting, wildlife viewing).
Sustainable industries like eco-tourism and outdoor gear.
Climate resilience, which protects jobs dependent on natural resources.
According to the U.S. Forest Service, outdoor recreation contributes $140 billion annually to the U.S. economy. Weakening the Roadless Rule would jeopardize these benefits and prioritize short-term profit over long-term sustainability.

5. A Moral Obligation to Future Generations
We have a moral responsibility to leave the world better than we found it. The Roadless Rule is a promise to future generations that we valued their right to a healthy planet over industrial exploitation. It ensures that:

Children can experience wild landscapes.
Wildlife can thrive without human encroachment.
Clean air and water remain accessible for all.
We cannot afford to break this promise.

Call to Action
I urge the USDA Forest Service and the Trump Administration to:

Uphold the Roadless Rule in its entirety without exemptions or loopholes.
Reject any efforts to weaken or undermine this critical conservation policy.
Prioritize science, Indigenous knowledge, and public input in all decisions affecting roadless areas.

Expand protections for additional roadless areas to ensure comprehensive conservation.
The Roadless Rule is not just a policy—it is a legacy of stewardship. Let us choose wisdom, compassion, and foresight. Let us protect these wild places for the health of our planet and the well-being of all who depend on them.

Sincerely,
Lilly Steward
3628 Oak Canyon Ln.
Vacaville, CA, 95688
lillysteward@icloud.com

I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (36 CFR Part 294, Subpart B), Docket No. FS-2025-0001, RIN 0596-AD66.

I love this country's national forests and wild places. I have spent time in them, and I know what it means to stand in a forest that has never seen a logging road. That experience cannot be manufactured or restored once it is gone. If this rescission goes through and roads are built and logging begins in these areas, we lose that land's wild character permanently. There is no undo button on a road cut through an inventoried roadless area.

This rule protects close to 60 million acres, nearly a third of the entire National Forest System, across 38 states and Puerto Rico. That is not a small regulatory tweak. It is one of the largest conservation actions in this country's history, and the public has said clearly and repeatedly that it wants these lands kept intact. Recent polling shows 76 percent of likely voters support keeping the Roadless Rule in place, with majorities across Republicans, Democrats, and independents. This is not a partisan issue. It is a question of whether the agency will listen to the people it serves or to the timber and extraction interests that stand to profit from opening these lands.

The stated justification for this rescission is wildfire risk. But the 2001 Rule already allows road construction and vegetation treatment for wildfire risk reduction and ecosystem restoration where it is genuinely needed. The Department's own numbers show that only about 5 percent of roadless areas have received hazardous fuels treatment since 2014, and that more than a quarter of these acres already sit near existing roads. That is not evidence that the rule is the barrier. It is evidence that fuel treatment work has been underfunded and understaffed, a problem rescinding this rule does not fix. Stripping protection from 44 million acres to address a treatment backlog that the rule itself does not prevent is not a solution. It is a pretext.

Beyond fire policy, these roadless areas are the backbone of clean drinking water for downstream communities, the last refuge for wildlife that cannot survive fragmented habitat, and the foundation of an outdoor recreation economy that depends on forests staying forests. Once roads and logging equipment go into an intact watershed, sediment and erosion follow, and they do not reverse when a logging contract ends.

I am asking the Forest Service to withdraw this proposed rescission and keep the 2001 Roadless Rule fully intact. If wildfire risk in specific high hazard areas is a genuine concern, address it through the exceptions the rule already provides, with real funding for fuel treatment crews, not by eliminating protection for tens of millions of acres nationwide. Timber and mining interests will always be able to make a case for opening more land. The job of this agency is to weigh that case against the public's clear and lasting interest in keeping some places wild, and I do not believe that balance favors rescission.

Thank you for considering this comment and for extending the comment period to allow for full public input.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the USDA's proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (36 CFR Part 294, Subpart B).

The 2001 Roadless Rule was established through one of the most extensive public engagement processes in the history of federal rulemaking, drawing 1.6 million comments with 97% of respondents in support of strong protections. The current proposal to rescind it runs counter to that overwhelming democratic consensus and should not move forward.

The 44.7 million acres protected under the Roadless Rule represent some of the most ecologically intact lands in the National Forest System. These areas provide critical wildlife habitat, clean drinking water for millions of Americans, carbon storage, and climate resilience. Once roads are built and timber is harvested in these areas, the damage is effectively irreversible. No local land management plan can adequately substitute for a consistent, national-level protection.

The USDA argues that returning decision-making to local forest officials will provide sufficient protection. I disagree. Shifting authority to individual forest plans creates a patchwork of inconsistent protections and places enormous pressure on under-resourced local offices. The history of roadless area management prior to 2001 demonstrates exactly why a national rule was necessary in the first place.

The USDA's own Tribal Summary Impact Statement documents that the majority of consulted Tribal governments oppose this rescission, citing threats to sacred sites, traditional gathering areas, water quality, and subsistence resources. The Federal Government has a trust responsibility to Tribal nations that cannot be dismissed in the name of deregulation.

The USDA cites wildfire risk as a justification for rescission, but roadless areas are not the problem, they are often part of the solution. Intact forests with undisturbed soils and natural hydrology are more resilient to fire and drought. Building roads into these areas fragments habitat, increases erosion, and introduces invasive species, ultimately worsening long-term forest health.

I urge the USDA and the Forest Service to reject this proposed rule and retain the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule in its entirety. The modest economic benefits projected from rescission, estimated at just $5–11 million per year in timber revenue, do not come close to justifying the permanent ecological, cultural, and public health costs.

As a wildlife biologist and spatial analyst, with a background of over a decade working in natural resources, I would like to affirm my objection to the removal of the United States Forest Service Roadless Rule. 

Roadless areas prevent accidental wildfires caused by anthropogenic activities such as legal or illegal camping, and vehicle presence (dragging chains while towing, hot engines igniting dry vegetation, etc.). Aplet et al. 2026 found that that land within 50 meters of a USFS forest road is up to four times more likely than roadless areas to have fire ignitions, because many fires are caused by human activity. The 2001 Rule itself (66 FR 3254) states that building roads into roadless areas would likely raise the chance of human-caused fires because more people would be present (USDA Forest Service, 2000). Wilderness areas may receive prescribed fire under some circumstances, particularly to reduce fire fuel loads, and roadless areas still receive natural fire caused by lightning. Roads and industrial logging do not prevent wildfire. The Roadless Rule contains exceptions that allow certain activities when necessary for public health and safety, and protecting resources. This includes forest management and hazardous fuels work.

Roadless areas help protect wildlife, not only because large tracts of intact habitat protect wildlife populations and clean water. The negative impacts that roads can have on terrestrial invertebrates are well documented, and include mortality from construction, vehicle collisions, changes in behavior such as nesting disturbance, increased human presence, the spread of invasive species and changes to the physical landscape (Trombulak & Frissell 2000). Even just the noise from motors causes disturbance to wildlife populations, reducing individual fitness and reducing the quality of habitat (Ware et al. 2015). 
In addition, Roadless areas provide human communities with downstream access to clean drinking water, and clean water supports freshwater fish, invertebrates, and amphibians. Building roads increases runoff and sedimentation in mountain streams (Gucinski et al. 2001) and negatively impacts aquatic connectivity for freshwater species (Wofford et al. 2005). 

The USFS has a notorious backlog of deferred road maintenance for the roughly 370,000 miles of roads that comprise the National Forst System road network. According to USFS’s Fiscal Year 2025, Quarter 2 Deferred Maintenance Needs report, the deferred maintenance value for passenger-vehicle roads is $5.89 billion, and that does not include high-clearance roads. Unmaintained roads and road bridges can lead to landslides and threaten aquatic connectivity and water quality. Why build new roads when USFS consistently fails to maintain the current inventory of roads and road bridges? If roads are built and then not maintained, then any claims about how the recission of the Roadless Rule alleviating management restrictions and improving public access are moot. If no sufficient budget exists for maintaining the current infrastructure, how will USFS plan and execute maintenance of additional road miles and road bridges? 

As someone who resides in and holds great esteem for the State of Georgia, I must point out that there are very few large tracts of contiguous wilderness left in the Southeastern United States. Unlike the western part of the country, we have no areas of vast, unbroken wilderness. The ability to go out into the wilderness and experience natural areas away from civilization and its sounds is a priceless thing. The protection of our cultural and natural resources in the Southeastern US is priceless.

I oppose the proposal to remove and reserve 36 CFR part 294, subpart B. I urge the Forest Service to withdraw it and keep the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule as it is.

1. The rule works and is settled. For 25 years it has kept road construction, reconstruction and timber harvest out of about 58.5 million acres of inventoried roadless areas, while allowing the exceptions the rule already contains for safety, access rights and other needs. It has been upheld by the federal appeals courts and has provided stable, predictable management. The notice does not identify any problem the rule has caused that justifies abandoning it.

2. Leaving decisions to individual forest plans is not equivalent protection. Forest plans are revised on long cycles, can be amended project by project, and vary widely in strength. Replacing one national standard with many local ones would expose these lands to piecemeal loss, with each decision looking small while the cumulative effect is large. The Idaho and Colorado state rules, which the notice leaves in place, show that a durable standard is workable; they are not a reason to remove the national one.

3. Roadless areas deliver benefits that new roads would put at risk. These lands protect headwaters and drinking water sources, intact habitat and wildlife corridors, and refuge for species that cannot tolerate fragmentation. They also serve hunting, fishing, hiking, backcountry skiing and other dispersed recreation that supports rural economies without major public investment.

4. The economic case is weak. The notice estimates a timber harvest increase of only 5 to 10 percent and Treasury and Forest Service revenue of about $5.2 to $11.4 million a year. That is small against the value of the protected lands and the long-term cost of building and maintaining new roads. The Forest Service has itself reported a very large road maintenance backlog, and adding roads in remote, steep terrain would add to it. New roads can also bring new human ignitions and invasive plants into remote areas.

5. The process is inadequate for a change of this scale. A rule that covers 58.5 million acres and was shaped by an extensive public record should not be rescinded on a short comment period. The draft environmental impact statement must fully analyze the cumulative effects on water, wildlife, climate and carbon storage, recreation and tribal interests, and must consider the no-action alternative on its merits.

I request that the agency adopt the no-action alternative, retain the 2001 Roadless Rule in full, and make no changes to its prohibitions or its definitions of inventoried roadless areas.

Respectfully submitted,

Francesco Franzini

To whom it may concern,

I am writing today to beg you to reconsider the rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule. Greenlighting development in protected wilderness areas will have dire consequences for the flora, fauna, and human communities that depend on them. The inherent, intrinsic value of protecting our wilderness far outweighs any “economic” value that can be extracted from plundering it for its natural resources. Development will come with a steep cost: the fragmentation of habitat that will result will threaten biodiversity and contribute to the worsening climate crisis and general degradation of the planet, ruining the environment for generations to come.

Ecosystems are fragile and complex, and they are already under threat from human activity, pollution and global warming. There are so few untouched wilderness areas left, and the Roadless Rule helps protect them. These areas will serve as vital refuge for endemic species whose very existence would be impossible without the ecosystems they evolved in. Running roads through these areas would damage habitat essential to the species that are most susceptible to a changing environment, leading to devastating losses of biodiversity (Nick M. Haddad et al’s “Habitat fragmentation and its lasting impact on Earth’s ecosystems”). Additionally, the introduction of pollutants from constructing these roads and running vehicles and increased foot-traffic through them will cause great harm as they enter root/soil, bodily, and water systems. The health of forestland and waterways will determine their ability to act as carbon sinks in this era of anthropogenic climate change; old growth forests are some of the best defenses we have against rising greenhouse gas emissions. Rescinding the Roadless Rule will cause irreparable damage to these already fragile ecosystems and introduce new problems that reduce these areas’ carbon capture potential and their ability to support life.

Under the Rationale section of this proposal, it acknowledges maintaining “ecological integrity,” mitigating wildfire risk, and increasing access for forest/insect/disease management purposes, while simultaneously highlighting the need to access timber and mineral resources. These ideals cannot coexist.  According to the language used in Donald Trump’s executive orders, especially E.O. 14153, it becomes clear that the true purpose of this proposal is for economic gain - the extraction and exploitation of the Earth’s precious materials. Roads often increase wildfire risk and decrease ecological integrity, as roads lead to traffic that can spawn wildfires from exhaust heat or sparks from metal scraping asphalt, rock, or other metal (Jennifer K Balch et al’s “Human-started wildfires expand the fire niche across the United States”). The increase in traffic can also lead to the movement of insects and disease, as the movement of people and cars can act as vectors that transport these. Lastly, the physical act of carving a road into the land can make it unstable, as this creates stress points and removes plants whose root systems were holding the land in place, leading to landslides. This does not sound like ecological integrity to me. Prosperity does not come from deregulation (EO 14192), destruction does.

I can think of nothing more unpatriotic than ruining our country’s wilderness - landscapes that inspire patriotism through songs like “America the Beautiful” (Katharine Lee Bates and Samuel A. Ward)  and “This Land Is Your Land” (Woody Guthrie). The language that is used in the executive orders that this proposal references paints a clear desire to access these lands for economic gain - an abuse of power that will undo the years of preservation granted by the Roadless Rule. 25 years ago, people foresaw the importance of protecting millions of acres of forestland, and this rule has been one of the most successful stories of land preservation this country has seen. Regulations like the 2001 Roadless Rule are put in place with good reason, researched and backed by experts.  That the advice of experts can be overridden by one man’s word is extremely disappointing.  Why does the Forest Service want to bend the knee to one man’s desires? The Roadless Rule was put into place to ensure that these areas could be enjoyed by everyone and continue to provide crucial habitat in a country whose landscape has already been poisoned and marred by the dangerous ideals of capitalistic growth.  There are already hundreds of thousands of miles of road running throughout this country’s national parks and forestlands, providing ample connectivity and access to nature for recreation, management purposes, and beyond. To remove federal regulation sets a dangerous precedent, allowing for untold damage to occur in its absence.

This land is for you and me; it is not for sale. Please protect the land, the water, and the people and animals that depend on them. Save the Roadless Rule

Date: October 6, 2026
To: Ecosystem Management Coordination, U.S. Department of Agriculture – Forest Service
Re: Docket No. FS-2025-0001 / RIN 0596-AD66 – Comments Opposing the Proposed Rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Special Areas; Roadless Area Conservation, 91 FR 53827)
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) and Forest Service’s proposed rulemaking titled Special Areas; Roadless Area Conservation, which seeks to fully or partially rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (36 CFR Part 294). I urge the agency to select Alternative 1 (No Action) and retain full protections for all ~58.5 million acres of Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs) across the National Forest System.
The 2001 Roadless Rule provides critical safeguards for intact, undeveloped backcountry habitats, water quality, and public recreation while allowing appropriate management flexibility. Removing or diluting these protections will produce severe, irreversible consequences for our public lands:
 * Ecosystem Integrity and Biodiversity: Inventoried roadless areas serve as essential strongholds for thousands of fish and wildlife species, including endangered and threatened species requiring undisturbed habitat connectivity. Introducing new industrial road construction, timber harvesting, and resource extraction fragments these corridors and invites invasive species.
 * Watershed and Drinking Water Protection: Unroaded watersheds supply clean, filtered drinking water to millions of Americans and downstream communities. Developing roads in steep or fragile terrain dramatically increases soil erosion, runoff, and sediment loading in streams, raising municipal water treatment costs and degrading aquatic habitats.
 * Fiscal Responsibility and Infrastructure Backlog: The Forest Service already faces a multi-billion-dollar backlog in deferred maintenance on its existing ~370,000-mile road network. Adding new roads in remote backcountry terrain creates long-term financial liabilities for taxpayers and diverts scarce agency funding away from maintaining existing infrastructure.
 * Wildfire Management Flexibility: Contrary to claims that the Roadless Rule hinders forest management, the 2001 rule explicitly contains exceptions allowing emergency response, hazardous fuels reduction, public safety measures, and thin-and-burn operations near communities. Expanding permanent road networks into deep backcountry areas increases human-caused ignition risks without improving community safety.
 * Economic Value of Outdoor Recreation: Intact roadless areas support a multi-billion-dollar outdoor recreation economy, sustaining local small businesses, outfitters, and rural economies that rely on world-class hunting, fishing, hiking, and backcountry experiences.
Dismantling the Roadless Rule ignores decades of public consensus, Tribal consultation, and sound conservation science. For these reasons, I respectfully request that the Department withdraw the proposed rescission and maintain the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule in its entirety.
Thank you for considering these comments.

text:
Please do not rescind the Roadless Rule. It is grounded in sound science and longstanding Forest Service policy.

Strategically limiting new road construction protects natural resources while preserving the agency’s ability to respond to wildfire, support communities, and maintain necessary access. The Roadless Rule already allows emergency roads and limited small-diameter fuel treatments when needed for public safety, wildfire response, and ecosystem restoration.

Peer-reviewed science and federal data show that expanding road networks in roadless and backcountry portions of National Forests creates substantial environmental and fiscal costs while doing little to make forests safer.

1. More roads mean more human-caused wildfire ignitions.  
People start about 84% of U.S. wildfires, and ignitions are concentrated near roads, communities, and other areas of human activity. Vehicles, dragging chains, hot exhaust systems, sparks, cigarettes, campfires, and roadside recreation all create ignition opportunities. Lightning-caused fires are generally more remote. Because current wildfire strategy appropriately prioritizes communities and high-risk firesheds, permanent roads deep in remote areas often provide little additional suppression benefit while increasing the chance of new ignitions.

2. The Roadless Rule already allows emergency access and fuel treatment.  
Under 36 CFR 294.12, roads may be constructed when necessary to protect public health and safety from imminent threats such as wildfire. Under 36 CFR 294.13, limited timber cutting may occur to reduce the risk of uncharacteristic wildfire or improve habitat. Managers therefore retain needed tools without opening roadless country to extensive permanent road systems.

3. Forest roads damage watersheds.  
Decades of research show that unpaved forest roads increase erosion, fine-sediment delivery, drainage alteration, landslides, and culvert failures. These impacts degrade trout and salmon habitat and can threaten downstream water quality. Decommissioning unnecessary roads and correcting failing crossings measurably improves watersheds and fish passage.

4. Roads fragment wildlife habitat.  
Roads displace wide-ranging wildlife, increase human-wildlife encounters and mortality risk, and divide otherwise secure habitat into smaller fragments. Large intact backcountry areas have ecological value precisely because they remain relatively free of continuous motorized access.

5. Roads spread invasive plants.  
Road corridors and vehicles are major pathways for non-native plants. New roads create disturbed edges where invasive species establish and spread, increasing future control costs and, in some cases, increasing fine fuels.

6. The Forest Service already has more roads than it can adequately maintain.  
The agency manages roughly 380,000 miles of roads. As of FY2023, deferred road maintenance exceeded $5.3 billion, excluding additional bridge needs. Adding more roads increases liabilities and diverts limited funds from priority access, safety, watershed protection, and maintenance. Fewer well-maintained roads make more sense than a larger road system the agency cannot adequately monitor or maintain.

7. Roadless landscapes also have economic value.  
Undeveloped public lands support tourism, recreation, scenic quality, quiet, and dark skies. Peer-reviewed forecasting for the Colorado Plateau estimated that dark-sky tourism could generate $5.8 billion in visitor spending over ten years, support $2.4 billion in wages, and sustain more than 10,000 jobs annually across four states. Economic value is not limited to timber extraction or expanded road access.

Rather than rescinding the Roadless Rule, the Forest Service should:

• Prioritize maintenance and safety improvements on existing roads serving communities, firefighting, and restoration.  
• Focus fuel treatments and all-hazards access in the wildland-urban interface and other high-risk firesheds.  
• Use temporary roads only where necessary and promptly restore them afterward.  
• Invest in Legacy Roads & Trails projects to remove unnecessary roads, replace failing culverts, and restore aquatic passage.  
• Maintain motorized recreation on sustainable routes identified through travel-management planning while protecting secure backcountry habitat, clean water, and intact ecosystems.

Rescinding the Roadless Rule would not solve wildfire, access, or forest-management problems. It would instead increase ecological impacts and deepen an already substantial maintenance burden. The more prudent policy is to maintain a limited, strategic, and sustainable road system that serves genuine public and management needs without sacrificing the remaining intact areas of our National Forests.

I write to oppose rescinding the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (the Roadless Rule). The United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) has insufficient information to understand the effects this action will have upon the environment and local communities in areas of increased road development. 

Under the Supreme Court's decision in Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County, Colorado (Seven County), the USDA must evaluate environmental impacts that are reasonably foreseeable under a rule change. In its environmental impact statement, USDA did not fully consider the impacts of road development in previously undeveloped forest land on soil, air, and water quality; plant and animal communities, including threatened and endangered species; or forest health. USDA justified this omission because "it is uncertain if there would be any future project-level decisions, and what those decisions might entail." 

This argument is patently absurd. USDA proposes a rule that would allow the development of roads where road development was not previously allowed. It then claims uncertainty as to what projects would result from this proposal. To clarify this uncertainty, I suggest to the USDA that allowing the development of roads will result in road development projects. Road development is not only a reasonably foreseeable impact but a straightforwardly obvious impact of rescinding the Roadless Rule. USDA is therefore obligated by the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) to prepare a full environmental impact statement evaluating the likely consequences, possibility of mitigation, and alternatives to road development in previously roadless areas. 

USDA's justification for rescinding the Roadless Rule is to increase multiple-use opportunities and allow management for wildfires, insect and disease infestations, and community protection. While USDA may not be able to determine every road project that will occur if the Roadless Rule is rescinded, it can easily note areas currently in need of wildfire or disease management or where roads would increase multiple uses. In every such instance, a road would not be permitted under current regulations and would be permitted if the proposed rule were finalized. Each potential road development is therefore a reasonably foreseeable consequence of rescinding the Roadless Rule. The impacts of each must be included in an EIS under NEPA and Seven County. I request USDA identify a range of potential road development in currently roadless areas if the Roadless Rule is rescinded. I further request that, across this range, USDA assess the environmental impacts of road development development on soil, air, and water quality; plant and animal communities; and forest health. I finally request USDA fully consider the environmental impacts of road development on the environment and local communities in its consideration of rescinding the Roadless Rule. Without this full assessment, USDA lacks sufficient information to ascertain whether rescinding the Roadless Rule will actually achieve its purported goals. 

USDA's environmental impact statement declined to consider the impacts that this proposed rule, if finalized, would have upon the environment and local communities. Because USDA has not accounted for the impacts of road development in this rule intended to allow road development, I strongly oppose finalizing the proposed rule for Special Areas: Roadless Area Conservation, 2026 FR 16965.

To the U.S. Forest Service:

I write in strong support of rescinding the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, particularly as it applies to the Tongass National Forest. [Personal line, e.g.: "As a lifelong Alaskan who has worked for decades on resource development in this state, I have seen firsthand what this rule has cost Southeast Alaska communities."]

Rescission is consistent with Executive Order 14192, Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation, which directs agencies to remove overly complicated and burdensome barriers to American business and innovation. It also implements Executive Order 14153, Unleashing Alaska's Extraordinary Resource Potential, which specifically directs the Forest Service to exempt the Tongass from the Roadless Rule.

The Roadless Rule's blanket prohibitions were never necessary on the Tongass. When Congress enacted the National Forest Management Act in 1976, it established a forest planning process designed to weigh conservation and use on a forest-by-forest basis. That process is fully capable of protecting the Tongass's important ecological values without a one-size-fits-all national rule.

Congress has also already struck the balance on the Tongass. Before the Roadless Rule was adopted, Congress designated more than 6.6 million acres of the forest as Wilderness and other restrictive land use categories through the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA) and the Tongass Timber Reform Act (TTRA). The lands Congress left out of those designations were left out deliberately, so they could support local employment, including year-round timber manufacturing jobs in a region where almost no state or private timberland is available to supply the mills. The Roadless Rule effectively overrode that congressional judgment, and in doing so it conflicts with both ANILCA and TTRA.

The consequences have been severe. Sustainable timber harvests on the Tongass have plummeted, and timber employment in Southeast Alaska is now a fraction of what it was before the rule took effect. The loss of these jobs has damaged the social and economic fabric of communities that have few alternatives for year-round work.

The rule also stands in the way of mineral and energy development that matters to the entire nation. The Tongass is highly mineralized, including volcanogenic massive sulfide deposits that contain critical and rare earth minerals needed for national security. Southeast Alaska also has more than 200 potential hydropower sites that could provide clean, affordable, renewable power to the region.

Under the Roadless Rule, access to these resources depends on the subjective judgment of individual Forest Service officials. The "reasonable access" the rule guarantees to mining claims does not necessarily mean road access. A Forest Supervisor can instead require costly helicopter access, an outcome that the authors of the Mining Act of 1872 could never have contemplated. Leaving it to an individual official to decide what access is "reasonable," or when a road is "needed," creates uncertainty that discourages investment and fails to protect access rights established in law.

Finally, the practical footprint of rescission is modest. Rescinding the rule would make only about 186,000 additional acres of the 16.9-million-acre Tongass available for timber harvest, roughly 1 percent of the forest. That is a small and reasonable change that would restore the balance Congress intended and give Southeast Alaska communities a real chance at economic stability.

I urge the Forest Service to finalize rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule.

Sincerely,
Sarah Ward
Anchorage, AK
