I am writing to oppose the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. I urge the Forest Service to select the no-action alternative and keep national protections for inventoried roadless areas.

I rely on these lands personally:
I regularly climb, ski tour, and run in the North Cascades. Many of the places I rely on such as the Highway 20 corridor around Washington Pass and Blue Lake, the Sauk and Mountain Loop approaches to Glacier Peak, the south side of Mount Baker, and the Teanaway east of Snoqualmie Pass — lie outside designated Wilderness and are protected only by the Roadless Rule. The Wilderness areas themselves would remain, but the intact approach valleys and old-growth corridors that lead to them would not. Rescission would leave these areas vulnerable and limit protections and guaranteed public access. 

The wildfire rationale does not support rescission: The Department justifies rescission mainly by pointing to wildfire risk. The 2001 Rule already allows cutting small-diameter timber to reduce fuels and restore ecological conditions. It also allows road construction when needed to protect public health and safety in cases of imminent threat. Most wildfires are ignited by people, and ignitions are concentrated near roads, so building new roads into remote backcountry is more likely to increase fire starts than to reduce them. The draft EIS should show, with data, how many fuel-reduction projects the Rule has actually prevented. If it cannot, the fire rationale does not justify removing protections from tens of millions of acres.

The Forest Service cannot maintain the roads it already has: The agency has a multibillion-dollar deferred maintenance backlog on its existing road system. Poorly maintained roads are a major source of sediment in streams, and they wash out and cut off access. Adding new road miles to a system the agency already cannot afford to maintain is fiscally irresponsible. The cost-benefit analysis should fully account for long-term road maintenance liabilities.

Roadless areas protect drinking water and fish habitat: Roadless areas include many headwaters that supply municipal drinking water and cold, clean water for salmon and other native fish. In Washington, salmon recovery is a legal obligation and a significant public investment. The draft EIS should quantify the effects on source water protection areas and on habitat for ESA-listed fish in each affected region.

"Local control" means uneven, reversible protection: Under the proposal, the national prohibition would be removed, and decisions about roads and timber harvesting would be made locally through each national forest's land management plan. Protection would then depend on which forest a place happens to be in and on how its plan is revised in the future. These are national forests owned by all Americans, and a consistent national standard is appropriate. 

Tribal nations oppose this rescission: The Department's own summary of consultation found that the majority sentiment among Tribal governments consulted is opposition to the proposed rescission, viewing it as a threat to inherent rights, Tribal sovereignty, cultural survival, and the ecological health of ancestral homelands. The Forest Service should not finalize a rule that most consulted Tribes oppose without resolving those concerns. 

The public process has been inadequate: The original Rule was developed through hundreds of public meetings and drew more than a million public comments. This rescission has had a short comment period and no public hearings. I ask the Forest Service to hold public hearings in affected regions, including the Pacific Northwest, before taking any final action.

Roadless areas support clean water, wildlife, carbon storage, and a recreation economy that depends on wild country. I urge the Forest Service to withdraw the proposed rescission and keep the 2001 Roadless Rule in place.

Sincerely,
Matt Stephens
Seattle, WA

Public Comment on Proposed Rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule
I am writing in support of maintaining the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule and in opposition to the proposed rescission.
My perspective is shaped both by my work in sustainable business and environmental policy and by a lifetime of experiencing America’s public lands. I have now visited 52 of our national parks, along with many national forests and other public lands across the country. Those experiences have reinforced for me that intact public lands are not simply scenic amenities. They are economic assets, natural infrastructure, and part of the long-term competitive strength of rural communities.
The proposed rule would rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule, which currently limits road construction, road reconstruction and timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas. USDA has extended the public comment period through October 6, 2026. Federal Register Public Inspection
I support the position of the American Sustainable Business Network that these protections should remain in place.
Roadless areas support outdoor recreation, tourism, hunting, fishing, clean water, wildlife habitat and the businesses that depend on those resources. Outfitters, guides, lodging operators, restaurants, breweries, retailers and many other small businesses benefit from landscapes that remain healthy, accessible and attractive over the long term. Once roads and associated development fragment those areas, the economic and environmental costs can persist for generations.
There is also an important fiscal question. Building new roads creates future obligations for maintenance, repair and eventual reconstruction. Public-land decisions should account not only for the near-term value of new development, but also for the long-term costs that taxpayers may inherit.
I also urge the Forest Service to carefully examine the claim that rescinding the Roadless Rule is necessary to improve wildfire management. A 2020 Forest Service-supported analysis of nearly two decades of monitoring found that roadless status had not prevented fuel-management activities, that forests with and without roads had burned at similar rates, and that the evidence did not support the assumption that removing road restrictions would improve overall forest health. The study also found a strong association between roads and the spread of invasive plant species. USFS Research & Development
That does not mean wildfire risk should be ignored. It means wildfire mitigation should be based on evidence and targeted management rather than used as a broad rationale for eliminating a national conservation standard.
A consistent national rule also provides value in its own right. Replacing the Roadless Rule with a forest-by-forest approach could create greater uncertainty, inconsistent protections and more pressure for piecemeal decisions. Businesses make better long-term decisions when the rules governing important public assets are clear and durable.
America’s public lands support recreation, tourism, clean water, healthy forests and rural economies precisely because previous generations made choices to protect them.
Having traveled extensively through our national parks and public lands, I have seen firsthand that their value extends far beyond their boundaries. They sustain communities, businesses, watersheds and experiences that cannot simply be recreated once they are lost.
I respectfully urge the U.S. Forest Service to retain the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule and continue protecting inventoried roadless areas as long-term economic, environmental and public assets.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
John Imes
Wisconsin

text:
Purpose and Need for Action
“The Department is proposing to rescind the Roadless Rule (issued in 2001) to reduce regulatory burden and return land management decision-making for inventoried roadless areas to local Forest Service officials. This approach prioritizes decision making by local Forest Service officials informed by Tribes, State, and local communities. As explained below, there is a need to increase local management flexibility and, where necessary, allow for active management to respond to changing and localized conditions, such as increasing wildfire risk, the spread of insect and disease infestations, and the need for community protection in the wildland-urban interface.”
The Draft EIS specifies three alternatives: 
1.	No Action -- Continue 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule on 44. 7 million acres
2.    2001 Roadless Rule Recission -- Repeal the Roadless Rule
3.    Modify the Roadless Rule – Remove Roadless Rule on 31.7 million acres
I favor Alternative 1: DO NOT RESCIND CURRENT ROADLESS RULE.
As a former USFS employee for many years with experience in land and wildlife management across the western United States, here are my reasons:
Reasons: 
1.	The Forest Service has a broad responsibility to manage multiple values and uses under its statutory mission, as well as other statutes such as Endangered Species Act and Clean Water Act. As the system of roads on Forest Service lands expanded greatly during the 20th century to 370,000 miles mainly to harvest timber and extract oil & gas, associated wildlands disappeared concurrently. I and many people value roadless areas for non-material benefits such as family recreation, protection of headwater watersheds for clean drinking water, hunting and fishing, and conservation of threatened fish and wildlife. The booming recreation in the backcountry also provides economic benefits to local communities and economies across the country. Roadless areas provide vital habitat and security for a diverse community of fish and wildlife species – including threatened species such as bull trout, grizzly bears, wolverines, and icons like elk and bighorn sheep that rely on roadless areas. Removing protections would leave them vulnerable to disturbance by vehicles, displacement from key habitats, and killing/poaching.  Roadless areas also provide crucial habitat connectivity across the landscape. They provide refugia for fish and wildlife shifting to higher, cooler elevations as the climate becomes hotter. Roadless areas often harbor old-growth trees, which store greater amounts of carbon dioxide.  
2.	While reducing risk of fire near human communities is important, a broad executive proposal to reduce roadless area within 500 m of ‘urban communities’ seems arbitrary and capricious, and contrary to local information and professional experience. Moreover, the draft EIS acknowledges that the best-available science substantiates that risk of human-caused ignition of fires is increased by more roads. The boundary of ‘urban community’ is not defined in the proposed rule and appears open to various and confusing interpretations. More and more houses are being built on private lands within or adjacent to National Forest boundaries. In recent years, fire behavior has become more extreme and catastrophic due to climate change with droughts and strong winds. Aerial fire-fighting has become more and more important and effective, thereby reducing the need for extensive roads.

3.	Substantial decision-making authority already is placed in the hands of local District Rangers and Forest Supervisors. The U.S. Forest Service has a long and strong tradition of gathering local information and experience while maintaining a commitment to its national mandate. Rather than a sweeping effort and weak rationale to eliminate roadless areas, the U.S. Forest Service needs to resume its commitment to open public engagement – both local and national – under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).
Closing Thoughts:  As public lands, our National Forests are a national treasure. The Roadless Rule is not broken. It is not doing harm to our lands and waters; rather, it is protecting and sustaining their diversity and integrity. The Forest Service already has an approximately $6 billion deferred maintenance backlog on its vast network of roads. Building more roads into environmentally sensitive areas makes no economic sense. We should not destroy some of our last remaining wild country to subsidize road building so that timber and oil and gas companies can take over our public lands.

Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

The heavily wooded trails around Bellingham were, for a time, where I understood what calm felt like. I hiked them listening for birds, using an app to identify what I was hearing, watching for any wildlife that would appear precisely because the environment was undisturbed. Wildlife, I learned, only comes out if everything is calm. I am writing against the rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule because what that rule protects is the condition those encounters depend on, and what this proposal would remove is irreplaceable.

On birds specifically, the agency's own record states what road-building does to the species I go looking for. The DEIS cites the findings that bird richness declines with road presence in forested habitat, and that road-noise experiments in a roadless area cut bird abundance by over a quarter, with 31 percent of species avoiding the noise entirely. Washington alone holds 139 inventoried roadless areas totaling 2,014,832 acres. Opening those places to roads does not simply change a land-use category. It removes the quiet that makes them habitat. I ask that the agency explain, with specificity, how it weighs that quantified loss against any projected benefit of rescission, and that it respond on the record to the finding that nearly a third of species are displaced by road noise alone.

On water, the agency's own analysis makes the case against itself. Across the Pacific Northwest region, which includes Washington, 1,522 municipal water intakes sit in watersheds containing affected roadless areas. The agency has also found that roads and their facilities can produce up to 90 percent of the sediment from a timber sale. My question is the same one I have been asking since I first read this proposal: why are we trying to build roads that will pollute more of our precious drinking water, and how is this improving the quality of life for the American people? The agency should respond to that question directly.

On fire, the agency offers wildfire management as a rationale for rescission, and then its own draft environmental impact statement contradicts that rationale. The agency's own record states: "Building a road into a forest at high risk from uncharacteristic wildfire effects could increase the incidence of human-caused fires. A human-caused wildland fire is nearly five times more likely to occur on essentially roaded lands than on essentially unroaded lands." The agency must explain why the proposal departs from its own prior findings on fire occurrence, and reconcile the rescission with the ignition data in DEIS Table 21, which reports far higher fire density on roaded land than inside the affected roadless areas.

On economics, the numbers the agency has placed in its own record do not support the action it proposes to take. The agency acknowledges that "the total timber volume affected by this rule is less than 0.5 percent of total United States production, and the total oil and gas production from all National Forest System lands is currently about 0.4 percent of the current national production." Against that, the agency projects $5.2 to $11.4 million a year in timber revenue against recreation losses of at least $6.1 million a year, a net present value spanning negative $92 million to positive $199 million, and a road system already carrying a $6.9 billion maintenance backlog. The agency should reconcile that arithmetic with the stated rationale before proceeding.

On the question of a state-by-state approach replacing the national rule, the agency's own record notes that "the USDA discussed its dissatisfaction with the Roadless Rule and highlighted its rejection of the Roadless Rule's 'inflexible one-size-fits-all nationwide rulemaking approach.' 70 Fed.Reg. at 25,656." The Ninth Circuit has already reviewed that reasoning and found it wanting. The agency must explain how this proposal avoids the deficiencies the court identified the last time the agency substituted local decision-making for national protection.

Finally, the agency cites the finding that habitat fragmentation reduces biodiversity by 13 to 75 percent, and then applies that finding to nothing. The 40.1 million acres of potentially affected environment sit in the record with no projection attached. The agency should do that work before finalizing any decision.

A logged stand grows back. A road does not. The Forest Service held more than 600 public meetings and took 1.6 million comments to write this rule. It has held none to undo it. If I ever have children, I do not want them to have fewer wild spaces than I had. A child should be able to experience nature in person, and not have their only option be reading about wild spaces that existed before decisions like this one were made.

Sincerely,
Madeline Ballin
Danville, CA 
previously Bellingham, WA

text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

Long hikes in nature, away from development and into the quiet that wildlife depends on, are what I value most about the roadless areas the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule protects. I take those hikes to escape human influence entirely, to look for owls and hawks, to ride trails through our protected parks and spaces, and to kayak rivers and lakes that remain intact because roads and industry have not reached them. Rescinding this rule threatens all of that, and the agency's own analysis makes the harm plain while refusing to follow through on it.

The DEIS cites the finding that "habitat fragmentation reduces biodiversity by 13 to 75 percent." That range is wide, and the low end alone is serious. What the document does not do is carry that finding forward. No projection applies that fragmentation range to the 40.1 million acres of potentially affected environment. The owls and hawks I go looking for depend on interior habitat that road construction breaks apart. An agency that cites a number it intends to use must use it. I ask that the agency apply the cited fragmentation range to the 40.1 million acres and explain in the record how it reached whatever conclusion follows.

The same pattern appears with big game. The DEIS cites the finding that "elk survival rates increased during a road closure and decreased when the gates were removed (Cole 1997), and that elk avoid roads and select unroaded habitat." That finding is stated and then set aside. The document projects no population-level effect on big game anywhere. A statement that elk avoid roads and die more when roads open is not analysis. It is a starting point the agency declined to finish. The agency must project the effects on big game populations and hunter opportunity under each alternative and put those projections in the record.

Carbon is handled the same way. The DEIS cites the estimate that "these inventoried roadless areas contain about 5 percent of the stored forest carbon in the coterminous United States, roughly 0.9 billion metric tons." The document then concludes these lands will continue to sequester and store carbon, offering no analysis of what harvest and road construction would do to that stock. Stating a baseline and assuming it continues unchanged is not analysis of a proposed change. I ask that the agency quantify the change in carbon storage and sequestration under each alternative, and explain in plain terms how that conclusion survives the proposal it is supposed to evaluate.

The harm to species is the most serious gap. The agency's own biological assessment closes by stating: "Rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule will increase the likelihood of road construction and timber harvests occurring in locations previously considered inventoried roadless areas. In many cases the Forest Service anticipates this increased activity to adversely affect some ESA-listed species and their designated critical habitats." The DEIS tallies the determinations: "may affect, likely to adversely affect" for 327 ESA-listed species and 71 designated critical habitats. The rivers and lakes I kayak, the forested trails I ride, the habitat where I look for raptors, these places carry species the agency itself expects to be harmed. The phrase "anticipates" is the agency's own word. This is not speculation from outside the process; it is the agency's forecast of its own action's consequences. The proposal identifies mitigation for none of it. The agency must disclose, species by species, how the likely adverse effects its own biological assessments identify will be avoided or mitigated, and ESA consultation must be completed and published before any final rule issues.

The 2001 rule should be retained. The agency should not finalize any rescission until it has answered each of these analytical failures in the record.

Sincerely,
Samuel McKinnon
Memphis, TN

Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

The national forests are where I go to find wildlife. Black bears, mule deer, marmots, chipmunks: I travel around the country spending time in national forests and parks specifically for their recreational and nature-viewing opportunities. The proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule threatens the landscapes that make those opportunities possible, and the agency's own analysis raises questions it has not answered.

On wildfire, the agency's stated rationale cuts against itself. The DEIS records that "Building a road into a forest at high risk from uncharacteristic wildfire effects could increase the incidence of human-caused fires. A human-caused wildland fire is nearly five times more likely to occur on essentially roaded lands than on essentially unroaded lands." The proposal nonetheless advances rescission partly on wildfire and fuels management grounds. I ask that the agency explain why the proposal departs from its own prior findings on fire occurrence and fuel treatment in roadless areas, and that it reconcile the rescission with the ignition data in its own DEIS Table 21, which reports far higher fire density on roaded land than inside the affected roadless areas.

The mule deer I look for in national forests depend on intact, unroaded country in ways the agency's own cited research makes clear. The DEIS cites Wyoming research finding that roads built for oil extraction may have altered mule deer migration routes and increased their movement speed. The agency's Tribal Summary Impact Statement credits the rule's protection with the recovery of deer and moose populations in Alaska by preserving old-growth winter shelter. And the DEIS records that "The DEIS cites the finding that elk survival rates increased during a road closure and decreased when the gates were removed (Cole 1997), and that elk avoid roads and select unroaded habitat." Despite holding all of this in its own record, the agency projects no population-level effect on big game anywhere in the document. I ask that the agency project the effects on big game populations and hunter opportunity before finalizing any action.

Bears raise a related concern. The DEIS draws on the federal grizzly recovery plan to note that increased contact and conflict from open roads in grizzly habitat can ultimately end in grizzly mortality, and that shooting, habituation, and food reward all increase with the use of even secondary unpaved roads. When I travel national forests to find black bears, the value of that experience depends on populations that are not being pushed toward conflict by road access. The agency has not projected how rescission would affect bear populations or the viewing opportunities that draw people like me to these lands. That gap deserves a direct answer in the final record.

The fragmentation evidence the agency cited quantifies the stakes but is never applied to the lands in question. The DEIS records that "The DEIS cites the finding that habitat fragmentation reduces biodiversity by 13 to 75 percent." That range is wide and consequential, yet no projection across the 40.1 million acres of potentially affected environment follows from it. The agency should apply the cited fragmentation range to those 40.1 million acres before drawing any conclusion about the tradeoffs involved.

Finally, the carbon accounting is incomplete. The DEIS states that "these inventoried roadless areas contain about 5 percent of the stored forest carbon in the coterminous United States, roughly 0.9 billion metric tons," and concludes these lands will continue to sequester and store carbon. That conclusion does not survive contact with the proposal: harvest and roading release stored carbon, and the document contains no analysis of how much would be released under any alternative. The agency must quantify the change in carbon storage and sequestration under each alternative it is considering.

The agency's own record contains the data needed to answer each of these questions. What it lacks is the analysis that would connect that data to a reasoned choice. I oppose the rescission and ask that the agency address each of these points before it proceeds.

Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

The land is ours. Once it is gone, it's gone, and there are fewer places left. I am submitting these comments in opposition to the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001, because what the agency is proposing to undo cannot be rebuilt once it is lost.

I hike to be outside in nature. It is good for the soul. I look for wildlife and birds, and I believe the wildlife needs its space. The agency's own data make clear what opening these areas to roads does to birds specifically: the DEIS cites the findings that bird richness declines with road presence in forested habitat, and that road-noise experiments in a roadless area cut bird abundance by over a quarter, with 31 percent of species avoiding the noise entirely. (Kroeger et al. 2022; McClure et al. 2013; Ware et al.) That is not a marginal effect. The agency must explain, in its response to these comments, how it expects bird communities to be protected across the affected landscape if this rule is rescinded.

The DEIS cites the finding that habitat fragmentation reduces biodiversity by 13 to 75 percent. That range is cited and then set aside. No projection of what it means across 40.1 million acres of potentially affected environment appears anywhere in the document. I ask that the agency apply that cited fragmentation range to the full 40.1 million acres before this rulemaking goes any further.

The agency's own citation addresses what roads do to large animals too. The DEIS cites the finding that elk survival rates increased during a road closure and decreased when the gates were removed (Cole 1997), and that elk avoid roads and select unroaded habitat. That finding is noted and dropped. No population-level projection follows. The agency should project the effects on big game populations and hunter opportunity under each alternative and put that analysis before the public.

I have been on mountain roads that were dangerous because they were not maintained. It does not make sense to spend money to build more roads when there is not enough money to maintain the ones that already exist. Beyond the dollars, roads carry sediment. The agency's own analysis says roads and their facilities can produce up to 90 percent of the sediment from a timber sale, and more than 7,000 municipal water intakes sit in watersheds fed by these roadless areas. Keep our watersheds clean. Fewer than 12 percent of those watersheds have impaired streams today, and the agency should explain on the record how that number will not grow if road construction is permitted to expand into country that has none.

On carbon: The DEIS cites the estimate that these inventoried roadless areas contain about 5 percent of the stored forest carbon in the coterminous United States, roughly 0.9 billion metric tons. The document then concludes the lands will continue to sequester and store carbon, with no analysis of what harvest and roading would change. That is not analysis, it is assumption. The agency must quantify the change in carbon storage and sequestration under each alternative.

The most serious failure in this record is what the agency's own biological assessment finds and then proposes to do nothing about. The agency's 428-page draft biological assessment closes: "Rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule will increase the likelihood of road construction and timber harvests occurring in locations previously considered inventoried roadless areas. In many cases the Forest Service anticipates this increased activity to adversely affect some ESA-listed species and their designated critical habitats." The DEIS tallies the determinations: "may affect, likely to adversely affect" for 327 ESA-listed species and 71 designated critical habitats. The agency wrote those words. It anticipates the harm and proposes no mitigation. I ask that the agency disclose, species by species, how the likely adverse effects its own biological assessments identify will be avoided or mitigated, and that ESA consultation be completed and published before any final rule is issued.

We need to stop developing every inch of the forest so our kids can know it. The Forest Service held more than 600 public meetings and took 1.6 million comments to write this rule. It has held none to undo it. A logged stand grows back. A road does not. The smoke from fire season is already so bad that you cannot go outside in town, cannot open windows, and it reaches people many miles from any fire. These lands filter water, hold carbon, and give wildlife the space it needs. They are not ours to spend. They belong to future generations too, and the agency should manage them that way.

Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

The animals that make the forest and this world beautiful, as I put it, are exactly what is at stake here. I watch squirrels, rabbits, deer and woodpeckers, and I know that what keeps those animals present and visible is the unroaded country this rule has protected. This proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule would end that protection, and I oppose it.

The agency's own record documents what new roads do to deer. The DEIS cites Wyoming research finding roads built for oil extraction may have altered mule deer migration routes and increased their movement speed (Sawyer et al. 2013), and the Tribal Summary Impact Statement credits the rule's protection with the recovery of deer and moose populations in Alaska by preserving old-growth winter shelter. Both findings are already in the record. Yet the proposal projects no population-level effect on deer or any other big game anywhere in the document. The DEIS cites the finding that elk survival rates increased during a road closure and decreased when the gates were removed (Cole 1997), and that elk avoid roads and select unroaded habitat. That finding also goes unextended into any actual projection. I ask that the agency project the effects on big game populations and hunter opportunity before this proceeding moves forward.

The wildfire rationale offered for rescission is harder to understand than anything else in this proposal. The agency's own record states: "Building a road into a forest at high risk from uncharacteristic wildfire effects could increase the incidence of human-caused fires. A human-caused wildland fire is nearly five times more likely to occur on essentially roaded lands than on essentially unroaded lands." The proposal nonetheless advances fuels management as a reason to open roadless areas to new construction. The agency must explain why this proposal departs from its own prior findings, and must reconcile the rescission with the ignition data in its own DEIS Table 21, which reports far higher fire density on roaded land than inside the affected roadless areas.

On the economics, the agency's record states that "the total timber volume affected by this rule is less than 0.5 percent of total United States production, and the total oil and gas production from all National Forest System lands is currently about 0.4 percent of the current national production." My own view is direct: they only want to build new roads to extract money, and it is ridiculous to squander nature for selfish gain. The numbers in the record support that skepticism. The agency's own Cost Benefit Analysis projects $5.2 to $11.4 million a year in timber revenue to the Forest Service against recreation losses of at least $6.1 million a year, with a net present value spanning -$92 million to +$199 million. That range cannot establish a net benefit. The proposal must be reconciled with those figures, and the agency must explain how expanding a road system already carrying a $6.9 billion maintenance backlog is justified when its own analysis cannot show the action pays.

The DEIS cites the finding that habitat fragmentation reduces biodiversity by 13 to 75 percent. That range is stark, and the 40.1 million acres of potentially affected environment make it consequential. No projection carrying that fragmentation range across those acres appears anywhere in the document. The agency should apply the cited fragmentation range to the 40.1 million acres before any final decision is made.

The animals I watch depend on country that roads would compromise. The agency's own record, on fire, on fragmentation, on deer migration and elk survival, on economics, does not support this rescission. I ask that the record reflect these objections and that responses to each be provided before any final action is taken.

Sincerely,
an american

As a citizen, I reject the proposal outlined in docket # FS-2025-0001. 

My concerns are simple: the administration is talking out of both sides of its mouth. This proposal states that the purpose is “intended to return primary authority for determining the appropriate management of inventoried roadless areas at the local level to the land management planning process.” However, since March of 2026, the administration has been playing with staffing locations. How is the proposal supposed to be taken seriously when, as reported in The Hill, the Forest Service is being moved to Utah due to “a ‘sweeping restructuring’ at the agency” (https://thehill.com/policy/energy-environment/5809780-trump-us-forest-service-hq-salt-lake-city-utah/). Then, at the beginning of September, the administration stated that 23 Forest Service office locations would be closed (https://thehill.com/policy/energy-environment/6070479-forest-service-closes-research-sites/). Per NPR, “(m)ore than 1,000 Forest Service employees work in hundreds of Research and Development facilities and structures located across the country. Staff work out of greenhouses, laboratories and cabins in urban areas like Baltimore and in more rural offices near the 193 million acres of national forest and grassland that the agency manages.” Boots on the ground that know the lands and ecosystems they oversee is very important. This proposal claims that these boots on the ground employees will be providing the necessary insight for roads etc but this administration is fickle. This administration is pushing to see what can be sold off at the expense of the people and lands it is supposed to care for. 

Additionally, the proposal does not weigh in on the accounting. There are some numbers provided for possible timber production but not for new roads/existing road maintenance. The same NPR article quoted above, also states that “President Donald Trump's 2027 budget proposed allocating $0 for Forest Service research, down from $309 million in 2026.” (https://www.npr.org/2026/06/06/nx-s1-5831470/forest-service-cuts). How are Forest Service staff supposed to determine this proposed rulemaking when they don’t know where they work and have no budget???? The Washington Post states, “one of the primary and still valid reasons the [roadless] rule was passed in 2001: The Forest Service can’t afford to maintain the roads it already has… the Forest Service currently lacks the capacity to maintain roads and conduct wildfire mitigation and forest restoration projects at the scale needed.”(https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2026/10/01/roadless-rule-has-lesson-america-forests/). Instead of rolling back the roadless rule, the administration should be putting forward rules and regulations to combat climate change and increasing budgets to ensure the best possible outcomes for the longer lasting wildfire seasons. 

I care for my countries public lands and wildlife. Why is the administration putting forward this proposal when they know it will cause more harm than good? I reiterate my objection to this proposal.

I do not support the USDA’s proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule. I recommend the USDA pursue Alternative 1 - NO ACTION. 

According to the Department’s rationale for the proposal, the “national blanket management approach… constrains responsible officials from exercising the timely, place-based discretion needed to meet the Forest Service's multiple-use mission.” 

Response: Adequate funding and sufficient personnel are greater constraints than place-based discretion. This presidential administration has repeatedly restructured the Department, cut funding and otherwise hampered the Department’s ability to execute on its goals. Continuing to push federal responsibilities onto states and other management entities misrepresents the federal government’s continued choice to inadequately fund public land management.

According to the Department’s summary of potential impacts, “Rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule would increase opportunities for hazardous fuel treatments in the wildland-urban interface.” 

Response: Again, there is no evidence that the Department, supporting federal departments/agencies, or state-based organizations have additional funding or capacity to take on such hazardous fuel treatments. Additionally, research shows that the majority of wildfires start within a half-mile of a road and are human-caused. Referencing data from the National Interagency Fire Center analyzed by OnX Maps, only 3% of all mapped historical wildfire ignition points over the last 50 years have occurred within Roadless Rule areas.

Hinging this proposal on improved wildfire management fundamentally misrepresents the impact of additional hazardous fuel treatments on overall wildfire activity, even in Western States where the majority of these Roadless Areas reside. 

I was born and raised in California, and I am a homeowner. Nearly every year of my life, I have prepared to evacuate, left my home, and or prepared to physically fight wildfire myself alongside our incredible first responders. The claims made in this proposal do not target the cause of recent wildfires our state has experienced, or those experienced across the southwest.

According to the Department’s summary of potential impacts, “Some industries, including recreation and tourism, could experience trade-offs as a result of the proposed rule.” The summary also acknowledges that “there is additional flexibility for potential future leasable mineral development (primarily oil, gas, and coal) opportunities and it is reasonably foreseeable that some development could occur in potentially affected inventoried roadless areas.”

Response: Recreation is not just important for American’s well-being, it also holds monetary value. The total economic output, or value of all sales associated with hunting, angling and wildlife-watching on BLM lands, was more than $3 billion in 2016, according to Pew.org (California: The Economic Contributions of Hunting, Fishing, and Wildlife-Watching on BLM Lands. US Forest Service lands hold similar value. There is additional significant, unquantified value of these lands with respect to hedonic price functions, property value and overall quality of life, as explored in the 2010 study [THE ECONOMIC VALUE OF PROTECTING INVENTORIED ROADLESS AREAS: A SPATIAL HEDONIC PRICE STUDY IN NEW MEXICO]. According to this study, there is a 5.6% gain in the property value of a house from being located in, or adjacent to, a Census tract with IRAs.

I urge the USDA to carefully consider the individual impact of rescinding the Roadless Rule and how additional development will impact homeowners across the Southwest.

In summary, I do not support the USDA’s proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule. I recommend the USDA pursue Alternative 1 - NO ACTION.

The Wallowas, Joseph Canyon, the upper John Day, the deep river country draining toward the Snake. Old ponderosa pine, Douglas fir and western larch that survived generations of logging and now stand in some of the last remaining old-growth forest east of the Cascades. These are some of Oregon's great forests, and I hike and camp in them. The proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule threatens what makes them worth entering.

The agency's stated rationale for rescission includes forest health, but its own document undercuts that rationale. The notice claims that "The 2001 Roadless Rule limited the Forest Service's ability to conduct vegetation management within inventoried roadless areas and has contributed to the lack of active management of the national forests, which has contributed to challenges in addressing forest health concerns," as stated in the Rationale for the Proposed Rule. Yet the same document cites research finding the rule did not meaningfully constrain fuel treatments as a share of forested land, and notes that insect and disease risk in western roadless areas is similar to or lower than on managed forest land. The agency cannot have it both ways: either the rule was a meaningful barrier to addressing forest health or it was not. The agency must reconcile the forest health rationale with those internal findings before this rule proceeds.

The economic case for rescission is also thinner than presented. The document estimates, in the section on Economic Benefits from Recreation in Roadless Area Forests, that "Assuming an upper limit of a 1 percent annual loss of economic benefit within the likely operable and likely operable but complex areas translates into potential annual losses for trail and dispersed area recreation of $4.8 million and $1.3 million for wildlife-related recreation, nationally." That single-year ceiling is set against roadless recreation benefits of upwards of $1.5 billion, and the document itself concedes that the magnitude of losses is unknown. Roads and changed recreation settings accumulate and persist across decades, not just a single year, and the Recreation section acknowledges that roughly 52 percent of three setting classes are more likely to be affected. The place I hike and camp in is exactly the kind of dispersed, roadless country this analysis inadequately captures. The agency should estimate cumulative recreation losses over 20 years as roads and settings change permanently, and compare them with projected timber revenue, rather than relying on a one-year 1 percent ceiling as though roads can be unbuilt.

Most pressing is what the document discloses about the land that would actually be opened to harvest. In the section on Implications for Forest Vegetation, Health, and Carbon, the agency's own data state that "approximately 11-16 percent is old-growth forest, 54-63 percent is mature forest, and 26-31 percent is young forest" within the operable areas most likely to be logged under the proposed action. Old and mature stands together make up the overwhelming majority of that timberland. The document identifies no old-growth-specific safeguards beyond general land management plan compliance before these stands could be harvested. The forests I walk through east of the Cascades, the ones that survived previous logging rounds, are precisely this kind of old and mature timber. The Forest Service must separately analyze and publicly disclose what protections, if any, would apply specifically to old-growth and mature stands before any harvest is authorized in this land base. The document as written does not do that.

To the USDA Forest Service:

I am writing to oppose the rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. I was born and raised in Idaho and I currently live in Washington. As such, I grew up enjoying the outdoors and my favorite activities still include hiking, rafting, and back-packing.  

Why the rule exists. The Roadless Rule was adopted to protect the last large, undeveloped areas of the National Forest System, roughly 58.5 million acres. These landscapes provide intact wildlife habitat and clean water for downstream communities. Roads are a leading source of erosion and stream sedimentation, and poorly placed culverts block the fish migration that native trout and salmon need to survive. Roadless areas also contain much of the remaining old-growth forest, which stores large amounts of carbon that logging would release. The rule also reflected fiscal reality: the Forest Service already could not maintain its existing road network of hundreds of thousands of miles, and building more roads would add to that burden.

The strength of the public record. This was not a hasty rule. It was developed over years, with more than 600 public meetings and a 120-day comment period, and it drew about 1.6 million public comments, most in support. That was a record for any federal rulemaking at the time. Its durability since then speaks for itself. Colorado and Idaho have adopted state-specific roadless rules modeled on the national standard. By comparison, the current proposal provided 30 days for comment, later extended by only 15, while the Forest Service has traditionally allowed 60 to 90 days for a draft EIS of this magnitude. A decision affecting millions of acres deserves a comparable public process.

Harm to wildlife, fisheries, and communities. Species that need large blocks of undisturbed habitat, such as grizzly bears, wolverines, lynx, and elk, decline as road density rises. Cold-water fisheries depend on the clean, cold streams that roadless watersheds provide. Communities near these lands rely on them for drinking water, and many local economies depend on hunting, fishing, and recreation, which rest on undeveloped backcountry. Rescission would put all of these at risk, and the costs of road construction and maintenance would fall on taxpayers.

The wildfire justification does not hold up. The proposal presents rescission as necessary for wildfire management. But the existing rule already allows fuel-reduction and thinning projects where they are needed to protect communities. Rescission is not required to do this work. Roads also increase human-caused ignitions and spread invasive plants that can worsen fire conditions.

The real purpose appears to be timber. The rationale for rescission, taken as a whole, points to expanded logging in these areas. At the same time, the agency's own analysis acknowledges that the practical footprint would be limited, estimating about 4.8 million acres potentially available for timber because of terrain, access, and cost. If the real-world benefit is that modest, it cannot justify removing protections for tens of millions of acres, which would leave them exposed to future road building and development, for decades to come, and the increased risk to wildfire from human caused ignitions. 

I urge the Forest Service to retain the Roadless Rule, or at the very least to extend the comment period and hold public meetings before making a final decision.

Sincerely,
Mary Hamann, Seattle, WA

RE: RIN 0596-AD66, Docket FS-2025-0001

Thank you for the Forest Service's work to find ways to keep our national forests healthy, and for the chance to comment. I support Alternative 1 and ask the Department to keep the 2001 Roadless Rule in place.
I agree with the Department's diagnosis. Decades of fire suppression have built up fuels and closed canopies. I study butterflies and moths in the field around Clackamas and Multnomah Counties, and I see meadows filling in and open forest closing over without fire. Prescribed burning, managed wildfire and thinning are critical. Where I disagree is the prescription. New roads would make the Department's job harder.

The rule is not what stands in the way. It does not restrict prescribed fire, and it already allows small-diameter cutting to reduce wildfire risk and roads to meet imminent threats. The Forest Service's Rocky Mountain Research Station found there is already more fuel treatment per square kilometer inside roadless areas than elsewhere (Healey 2020). The limit is funding and crews.

A bright line is the cheapest answer. Today everyone knows the answer in a roadless area before spending a dollar. Rescission replaces that rule with a case-by-case "maybe" across about 44 million acres, decided forest by forest and likely litigated project by project. A "maybe" invites spending on long-shot roads and timber sales in remote, low-value country, and the public pays to prepare them: in the Tongass, 45 percent of timber sales offered from 1998 to 2007 drew no bids. Water providers, outfitters and recreation businesses have also relied on this rule for 25 years, and the final EIS should account for those reliance interests.

The agency cannot afford more roads. The draft EIS reports that appropriated funding for the road system has fallen almost 70 percent in twenty years. Every dollar spent on new roads is not spent on burning and thinning. Roads also add fire starts: the draft EIS's own data show ignitions concentrated near roads, and Oregon's own comments cite 53 percent more ignitions than expected within 200 meters of roads. At the road stubs I visit I find broken glass, trash, shotgun shells and long-term camps, a law enforcement and fire burden that new roads would carry into country that has none today.

Roads also bring invasive plants. The same Forest Service study found roads strongly associated with their spread (Healey 2020). This is a problem for everyone, including firefighters: invasive grasses such as cheatgrass cure early, fill the gaps between trees and shrubs, and carry fire faster and more often than the native plants they replace. Every new road is a new corridor for them into country that is mostly free of them today.

Alternative 3 is not a narrow fix. It drops 17.9 million acres because they lie near a road or in the wildland-urban interface, plus the entire Tongass and, by Oregon Wild's count, about three quarters of Oregon's roadless acres. The fire concern near communities is already covered by the rule's exceptions.

I ask that the final EIS (1) identify fire or safety projects the existing exceptions actually blocked, (2) state maintenance costs and funding for any road it expects to build or reopen, (3) explain why its goals cannot be met on roaded national forest land and the 104,000 miles of stored roads it already has, and (4) respond to the State of Oregon's comments asking for less than full repeal.

Please keep the Roadless Rule and put the resources new roads would take into prescribed fire capacity, crews and maintenance of existing roads. Thank you for considering these comments.

Dear Secretary and Chief:

As a resident who has spend all of their formative years in, and adjacent to roadless areas and the national forests of North Carolina, I am very familiar with the landscape and environment in a way that would be difficult to most without years of living in and observing the same location. I know what areas flood, what areas risk wildfires, what areas prevent sediment from ending up in creeks, and what animals depend on the environment. The ruling from 2001 holds a good role in ensuring order.

When I was growing up I always thought we were safe from wild fires despite living in the middle of the woods. I always had the assumption that the forests would be well managed and that the risk had been minimized. As I grew older and wild fires came within less than a mile of taking my family home, I came to know the problems that emerged as a result of a rapidly changing climate in the Western North Carolina area and repealing the 2001 ruling obviously wouldn't do us any favors.

I still remember seeing the orange glow of a forest fire lighting up the sky outside of my bedroom window on what would have otherwise been a pitch black night in my rural childhood home in Western North Carolina. The feeling of dread and helplessness knowing that there was essentially nothing I could do in that scenario left a lasting effect on me and I understood that anything that could increase the risk of forest fires is a threat to any rural community and the environment they call home.

“The highest wildfire-ignition density was in lands within 50 m of roads (7.99 fires/1000 ha), and the second highest wildfire-ignition density was in other national forest lands outside of the 50-m road buffers but not in wilderness or roadless areas (3.50 fires/1000 ha). Wildfire-ignition density was lowest in designated wilderness areas (1.75 fires/1000 hectares), followed closely by Inventoried Roadless Areas (1.97 fires/1000 ha). For human-caused, natural, and undetermined fires, wildfire-ignition density decreased as distance to road increased: in lands between 0 and 250 m from roads, 6 fires ignited per 1000 ha, whereas fewer than 2 fires ignited per 1000 ha at a distance class of over 2000 m from roads. — Fire Ecology (Springer Nature), 2026 (https://doi.org/10.1186/s42408-026-00450-2)”

The claim that building roads throughout national forests will 'reduce forest fires' is simply untrue. Almost of the forest fires in Western NC in recent history have been caused by human activity and heavily boosted in severity by changing climate. Building more roads within national forests only serves to increase the risk for human caused forest fires by allowing easier access and increasing human traffic in areas that would have otherwise been far less accessible.

All the best,

CommentID: RLC-20261006-7ZU7DZ

A forest isn’t something you can patch back together. Once a road cuts through it, the trees come out, the soil washes into the creek, and the quiet is gone for good. Once you amputate part of it, you can never get it back.

The administration says it needs to scrap this rule to fight wildfire. But roads don’t stop fires. Roads start them. The Forest Service’s own report finds that fires start about four times less often in roadless areas, and it admits any gain in fire prevention would be “modest.” The rule already lets crews thin forests and fight fires. Building roads to stop wildfires is like handing out matches to stop wildfires.

And that’s not all. The same report lays out the damage:

These forests feed watersheds that supply drinking water to about 24 million Americans, and repeal would bring more erosion, landslides, and mud into them.
The plan is “likely to adversely affect” 327 threatened and endangered species.
Nearby communities could lose up to $9 million a year in visitor spending.
Tribal nations consulted overwhelmingly oppose repeal, citing threats to sacred sites and treaty-protected hunting and fishing.
Your comment isn’t just shouting into the void. It’s evidence.

When the government changes a rule like this, everything the public submits goes into an official file called the docket. If the administration scraps the rule and conservation groups sue, that docket becomes the record a judge reviews. Courts don’t look at Instagram posts or protest signs. They look at what’s in the record.

The law says the agency has to respond to the major concerns the public raises. If we put the facts on the record and the agency ignores them, that becomes the heart of the legal case. They were warned, they had the proof, and they chose not to listen. Judges can throw out a rule for that. Courts also often refuse to consider an argument that nobody raised during the comment period. If it’s not in the docket, it may as well not exist.

Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

The woods my family hikes through are not a backdrop. They are a classroom, and I take my children there to find pileated woodpeckers, warblers and wrens, and to understand how a living ecosystem actually works. Ramseys Draft Addition in George Washington National Forest, Virginia, 12,781 acres of quiet forested land, is the kind of place that makes that teaching possible. Rescinding the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule would put it at risk, and this proposal does not justify that outcome.

The agency's own environmental record quantifies what roads do to birds: The DEIS cites the finding that habitat fragmentation reduces biodiversity by 13 to 75 percent. That range describes a range of futures, not a footnote, and it applies to 40.1 million acres of inventoried roadless land that this rescission would expose to new road construction. Virginia alone holds 64 inventoried roadless areas totaling 393,682 acres. The agency presents the fragmentation finding and then steps around it, offering no projection of how that biodiversity loss would distribute across the affected landscape. I ask that the agency apply the cited fragmentation range to the 40.1 million acres of potentially affected environment and explain what that means for bird communities like the ones my family seeks out in places like Ramseys Draft Addition.

The noise research sharpens the point further. The DEIS also cites the findings that road-noise experiments in a roadless area cut bird abundance by over a quarter, with 31 percent of species avoiding the noise entirely. Where new roads follow, the birds my child is learning to find will move or disappear. The agency must explain on the record how it weighs these documented acoustic effects against the claimed benefits of the proposed rescission.

The proposal substitutes state-specific management for one national rule, but the agency has been here before, and it did not go well. The record shows that the USDA discussed its dissatisfaction with the Roadless Rule and highlighted its rejection of the Roadless Rule's "inflexible 'one-size-fits-all' nationwide rulemaking approach." 70 Fed.Reg. at 25,656. What the record does not show is any explanation of how this proposal escapes the deficiencies that ended the last attempt at state-by-state replacement. The Ninth Circuit rejected that approach because incremental local decision-making erodes nationally significant roadless values before any single decision triggers meaningful review. I ask that the agency address its own prior finding that local decision-making can incrementally reduce nationally significant roadless values, and explain how this proposal avoids the deficiencies the Ninth Circuit identified the last time the agency replaced the national rule with a state-by-state approach.

There is also a carbon accounting problem that the DEIS raises and abandons. The DEIS cites the estimate that these inventoried roadless areas contain about 5 percent of the stored forest carbon in the coterminous United States, roughly 0.9 billion metric tons. After stating that figure, the document concludes that these lands will continue to sequester and store carbon, without analyzing what happens to storage and sequestration rates when harvest and roading become available options. A conclusion that large, resting on a number that significant, requires actual analysis. I ask that the agency quantify the change in carbon storage and sequestration under each alternative.

My family goes into these forests to learn something real. Ramseys Draft Addition and the broader network of inventoried roadless areas in Virginia represent an inheritance worth protecting with the rigor this proposal currently lacks. The agency should not finalize this rescission without first answering the analytical gaps identified above.

Sincerely,
Diana Lennon
New York State

To the USDA Forest Service:

I live in Tumalo, Central Oregon, between Bend and Sisters. Wildfire threatens my home, my property, and my livelihood. The Forest Service says rescinding the Roadless Rule will help with wildfire. I am writing to urge you to retain the rule in full (Alternative 1), because the evidence says rescission would make me less safe and would not address the real problem.

Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz says more than 40% of inventoried roadless areas have high or very high wildfire hazard potential, but that only 5% have received fuels reduction. That gap reflects what treatment is funded, not what the Roadless Rule permits, and the rule already allows fuel reduction. An agency that cannot maintain the roads it has will not become safer by taking on more of them. Public monies need to be spent on fuels reduction, not roads. 

For the last two summers, I have watched two large fires burn near my house. The Flat Fire in August 2025 burned about 23,000 acres two miles from Sisters, destroyed five homes, and threatened nearly 4,000. The Akawa Butte Fire in July 2026, started by lightning, burned about 27,000 acres northeast of Sisters. What stands between fires like these and my house is defensible space, hardened homes, and fuel treatment near communities, not new roads in remote backcountry. Rescinding protections across roughly 44.6 million acres would not have changed either fire, and it would pull money and attention away from the places where my community is actually at risk.

Most importantly, roads bring ignitions. People start the large majority of U.S. wildfires, about 84% in Balch et al. (PNAS, 2017), and ignitions concentrate where people can drive. New roads in currently roadless country would add ignition sources near communities like mine.

Fire and smoke are already costing me my livelihood. I run a short-term rental and my income depends on guests who come to Central Oregon for its forests, clean air, and outdoor recreation. In 2026, my bookings fell about30% during fire and smoke events because of smoke and closures. I am not alone. An Oregon State University analysis of Bend lodging data from 2021 to 2025 found that a sustained 10-point rise in August air quality index was associated with about $472,000 in lost lodging revenue, with losses growing as smoke persists. That analysis counted only lodging, not the restaurants, guides, and shops that depend on the same visitors. Because my livelihood rides on how this region handles wildfire, the Forest Service's wildfire case needs to be right. Money and attention spent on new road access in remote backcountry are not spent on the fuel treatment near communities that protects both homes and the local economy. My guests also come for the quiet, undeveloped backcountry the Roadless Rule protects. 

Roadless watersheds also protect my community's water. Bridge Creek, a tributary of Tumalo Creek, is Bend's main source of drinking water. It flows through the 14,829-acre Tumalo Mountain Roadless Area, which the Roadless Rule currently protects. Forest roads are a documented source of fine sediment to streams. A study of Oregon forest roads found that clearing vegetation from the cutslope and ditch increased sediment production about sevenfold (Luce & Black, Water Resources Research, 1999). Research in Oregon's Cascades found roads were a net source of sediment in the basins studied (Wemple et al., Earth Surface Processes and Landforms, 2001). Sediment degrades spawning habitat, warms streams, and raises treatment costs. New roads upstream of a municipal water supply would add crossings and culverts that will eventually fail, and downstream users and fish would pay for it.

Roadless lands protect wildlife. Roads fragment habitat and cut connectivity. For example, esearch at Oregon's Starkey Experimental Forest shows elk select habitat away from roads (Rowland et al., Journal of Wildlife Management, 2000). Central Oregon's migratory and sensitive species depend on intact core areas like Tumalo Mountain. Already, deer populations have dropped nearly 50% in the area where I lived. Rescinding the Roadless Rule will only further threaten this species, too--as well as countless others. 

Quiet and solitude are a public value. I specifically live in Central Oregon to hunt, hike, and ride in places where it is still quiet. Once a road is built, that character cannot be restored. Already, there are too many roads. 

I'll end by stating this process is inadequate. A 32-day comment period for a rule affecting tens of millions of acres is far shorter than the periods used when the rule was adopted and in the 2005 rescission attempt, which exceeded 120 days. A decision this large warrants a longer period and public meetings in affected regions, including Central Oregon.

I ask that you retain the Roadless Rule in its entirety and direct fire funding to fuel treatment adjacent to communities.

Sincerely,
Carrie Walker
Bend, Oregon

I am writing to oppose the full rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule and to urge the Department to select the No Action alternative. I am a hiker, hunter, angler, mountain biker and general outdoor enthusiast from Northern New Hampshire, and I have used national forest backcountry in many states.

1. Roadless areas support a far larger economy than extraction does.
The outdoor recreation economy generated $1.2 trillion in output in 2023, about 2.3% of GDP, and employed roughly 5 million workers. The logging industry, by comparison, generated about $15.7 billion and employed about 49,700 workers. Roadless areas include stretches of the Appalachian, Pacific Crest, and Continental Divide trails, as REI has noted, and the rural gateway communities near them depend on visitors who come for undeveloped backcountry. The final analysis should quantify how new roads and logging would affect recreation-dependent counties. It should not weigh only timber volume.

2. Roadless areas provide clean water and wildlife habitat.
More than 60 million Americans get drinking water from national forests, and roadless headwaters help keep that water clean. As The Nature Conservancy points out, these areas are habitat for wolves, grizzly bears, and salmon. The Forest Service's own 2001 analysis found that roadless areas benefit more than 220 threatened, endangered, or sensitive species. Roads fragment habitat and increase sediment and mortality. The Department should explain what has changed since 2001 to justify discarding those findings.

3. Roadless areas store carbon.
Roadless forests are estimated to hold about 445 million tons of sequestered carbon, much of it in old-growth stands. The Tongass alone holds roughly one-fifth of the carbon stored in all national forests. Logging releases that stored carbon, and the analysis should account for it.

4. Rescission is not needed for wildfire management, and roads could add to the maintenance burden.
The Department points to wildfire hazard in some roadless areas. But the 2001 Rule already contains exceptions for public health and safety and for hazardous fuel reduction, so rescinding the entire rule is not necessary to address fire risk. The Forest Service also carries a large road maintenance backlog. The final analysis should examine how many miles of new road it could afford to build and maintain, since more roads would add to that backlog.

5. The public process has been inadequate.
The 2001 Rule was developed through more than 600 public meetings, about 1.6 million comments, and a 129-day comment period. By contrast, the 2025 scoping period lasted only 21 days, and the comment period on this proposed rule and its Draft EIS was initially 32 days. In 2025 the Forest Service received over 600,000 scoping comments, with more than 99 percent opposing rescission. When a prior administration tried to rescind the Rule in 2005, the comment periods exceeded 100 days. The Council on Environmental Quality found that the median time from notice of intent to final EIS is 2.2 years, yet this process has moved in under one year. I urge the Department to hold in-person public meetings, particularly in affected rural and Alaskan communities and with Tribes, before any final decision.

6. The Rule reflects a durable balance.
The Roadless Rule has survived 25 years because it works: it leaves these lands open to hiking, hunting, fishing, camping, and many forms of motorized recreation, while protecting them from new roads and commercial logging. Alternatives short of full rescission can still be pursued where local needs require, but a nationwide rollback of roughly 45 million acres is unjustified.

I respectfully urge the Department to withdraw the proposed rescission and retain the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule.

Sincerely,
Evan Carmean
Sugar Hill, NH

Re: Docket FS-2025-0001 / RIN 0596-AD66 — Special Areas; Roadless Area Conservation (Proposed Rescission and Draft EIS)

As a private citizen, I oppose rescission. I urge USDA to adopt the No Action alternative and retain the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule.

1. My standing: I have visited national forests and parks in over a dozen states for hiking, camping, and recreation. Intact roadless forest is a large part of why these places are worth visiting. The local economies that depend on these visitors rely on the undeveloped character of these protected areas.

2. The rule protects irreplaceable resources. The 2001 Rule protects about 58.5 million acres from new road construction and most commercial timber harvest. These lands provide:
* Drinking water. Roughly 60 million Americans draw drinking water from national forest watersheds. Roadless watersheds filter naturally and avoid the sedimentation and chemical contamination that road networks cause.
* Habitat. Unfragmented forest and undammed, unlogged streams support salmon, trout, elk, and other species that depend on connected landscapes.
* Carbon and old growth. These areas hold significant remaining old-growth forest and stored carbon. Both take centuries to rebuild once lost.

3. The wildfire rationale is not supported by the record. The proposal frames the rule as a barrier to wildfire risk reduction. Yet research cited by conservation groups indicates wildfires are about four times more likely to start in roaded areas than in roadless ones. A separate study found that over 90% of fires start within half a mile of a road. Roads provide human ignition sources and spread invasive, flammable vegetation. The 2001 Rule already permits fuel-reduction work where needed, including cutting small-diameter timber to reduce hazardous fuels or restore ecosystems. The Final EIS must explain why that existing flexibility is insufficient, and the agency should not assume it.

4. Rescission is fiscally imprudent. The Forest Service already has a maintenance backlog for its existing road system, estimated at more than $8 billion. Opening 44.7 million acres to new road construction would add liabilities the agency cannot currently afford to maintain. Roads also carry well-documented ecological, hydrological, and health costs according to the Forest Service's own prior work (Gucinski et al 2001: https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/2922). The EIS should quantify the long-term maintenance costs of the roads that rescission would make eligible, including deferred-maintenance impacts on water quality and public safety.

5. The process is inadequate for the stakes. The 2001 Rule followed over 600 public meetings and about 1.8 million comments. This rescission was initially offered a 32-day comment period, extended only 15 days. That is far shorter than the periods offered when the Rule was created in 2001 and when it was previously revisited in 2005. A decision affecting 58.5 million acres in 39 states warrants a comparable record. I ask that the agency reopen or extend the comment period and hold public meetings in affected regions.

6. "Local decision-making" is not a substitute for a national baseline. The proposal states that rescission does not itself mandate logging or roads. But it removes the only durable, nationwide protection, leaving every roadless area vulnerable to case-by-case pressure and future project proposals. Forest plans can be amended, and irreversible harm can occur one project at a time. The Final EIS should analyze the cumulative effects, not just the effect of the rescission in isolation.

7. Irreversibility. A road cannot be undone in any meaningful ecological timeframe. Once built, a road changes hydrology, fragments habitat, and permanently alters public land. Given that asymmetry, the burden of proof should rest on those proposing to remove protection

Request: Select the No Action alternative and retain the 2001 Roadless Rule in full. If the agency proceeds, it should (a) extend the comment period and hold regional public meetings, (b) fully address the wildfire, water, cost, and cumulative-effects concerns above, and (c) fulfill all ESA, NEPA, and NHPA consultation obligations.

Respectfully, 
BR

I strongly object to ending the roadless rule. By ending this rule, it poses multiple threats to our forests and public health via increased wildfires, threatens local economies, jeopardizes clean drinking water for millions of Americans, threatens natural habitats and biodiversity, and violates the public land agreement with American taxpayers. 

Data shows that roads act as an ignition source for wildfires and they are the most common places for wildfires to start. The US Forest Service's own data shows that roads are highly correlated with wildfires, with the majority of wildfires being started as a result of human activity within 50 meters of a roadway. Additionally, researchers found that there is a four times greater risk of fires starting near roads compared with roadless forests (Aplet et al., 2026). The administration's claim that the Roadless Rule prevents the US Forest Service from decreasing wildfire damage is simply false; repealing this rule will result in more fires (Aplet et al., 2026), further straining already at capacity wildfire fighting resources. This also places habitats and communities in increased danger, and home and business owners assume an increased risk for property damage, which has further economic implications. Regarding public health, wildfire smoke contributes to poor air quality for millions of Americans. Wildfire smoke composition is harmful to breathe, exacerbating chronic respiratory conditions and promoting the development of reactive airway conditions, like asthma (The American Academy of Allergy, Asthma, and Immunology, 2026). The administration's continued cuts to healthcare spending creates a situation where we should be focusing on reducing chronic illness, not promoting it. The economic implications of long-term chronic conditions are well established, and air quality is a major factor in chronic disease prevention.

Local economies will suffer under this rule change, with the US Forest Service’s own economists stating that revoking the rule would result in a loss of up to $9 million annually in visitor spending to nearby communities that benefit from remote public land tourism. Additionally, the agency is already behind in existing road maintenance (US Forest Service, 2026); adding more dirt roads for the primary purpose of industry accessing forests, not for the benefit of American taxpayers, will further contribute to the road maintenance spending backlog resulting in an even bigger bill for taxpayers who are ultimately footing the bill for private industry to access our public lands (US Forest Service, 2026). 

Drinking water quality will suffer under this rule change for approximately 25 million Americans (Olden et al., 2026; US Forest Service, 2026). Increased soil erosion, sediment run off, and pollution will jeopardize remote watersheds that provide drinking water for millions of Americans (US Forest Service, 2026). At a time when we are facing more droughts and competition with industry for fresh water, this is a disastrous situation that will result in water shortages for millions of people. 

Additionally, the biological assessment provided by the US Forest Service highlights the negative impact on biodiversity and 327 threatened and endangered species. Seventy-one designated critical habitats are at risk with revoking this rule (US Forest Service, 2026). Biodiversity is the cornerstone of a healthy ecosystem. 

These lands are pristine and untouched American wilderness. Who are we that we would destroy our own world-renowned, iconic wilderness. This is our heritage. Americans take great pride in our protected, wild, public lands and I reject any actions by the federal government that would damage this, such as revoking the Roadless Rule. As an American taxpayer I fundamentally oppose this action that would result in unnecessary increased spending of our tax dollars, poorer air and water quality, destruction of old growth habitats and wildlife populations, and what represents an egregious misuse of our public lands with nothing in return, while industry makes billions in profits at our expense. I oppose.

Aplet, G.H., Hartger, P. & Dietz, M.S. Three-decade record of contiguous-U.S. national forest wildfires indicates increased density of ignitions near roads. Fire Ecology 22, 8 (2026). https://doi.org/10.1186/s42408-026-00450-2

Olden JD, Postel SL, Dombeck MP, Kesting H, Freeman P, et al. (2026) Assessing the value of the U.S. Roadless Rule for people and nature. PLOS Water 5(7): e0000538. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pwat.0000538
